[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 5.7 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"9eb313","wall_time_seconds":5.5144129,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":9469,"output":"  return <>\\r\\n    {!roles && <>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"One condition tells you something else\\">\\r\\n        <p>A <strong>condition</strong> is something we\'re considering. A door is open. A person has a ticket. An order has been packed. We can ask whether each one is true.</p>\\r\\n        <p>A <strong>conditional statement</strong> connects two conditions. It tells us that if one is true, the other has to be true too. It doesn\'t tell us that the first condition actually occurred. It tells us what would follow <strong className=\\"co-if-inline\\">if</strong> it did.</p>\\r\\n        <p>Think of that if as an invitation to imagine a situation. Suppose the first condition is true. What would you then know? We can ask that question without claiming the situation really happened.</p>\\r\\n        <IfConnection/>\\r\\n        <p>You don\'t need symbols yet. First, understand what the sentence is saying.</p>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Why learn this?\\" dark>\\r\\n        <p>An LSAT question gives you some information and asks what you can conclude from it. Sometimes that information is a rule about what has to be true if something else is true. You need to know what the rule says before using it.</p>\\r\\n        <p>A rule can tell you something about an order, a person, or a decision. It can also leave questions unanswered. We\'ll practice telling the difference between what we\'ve been told and what we\'re adding ourselves.</p>\\r\\n        <p>Let\'s begin with one rule. We\'ll read it, imagine a case that meets its condition, and ask what we know about that same case.</p>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Read one rule in ordinary English\\">\\r\\n        <blockquote>If an order is marked ready for pickup, it has been packed.</blockquote>\\r\\n        <p>There are two ideas here: an order is <strong>marked ready for pickup</strong>, and it <strong>has been packed</strong>. The sentence connects them. Imagine an order with that ready label. The rule tells you it has been packed.</p>\\r\\n        <p>We haven\'t been told that any particular order has that label. We\'re saying what would be true <strong>if</strong> it did. That\'s the difference between a rule and a fact about an actual order.</p>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Enough on one side, required on the other\\">\\r\\n        <p>Suppose an order is marked ready for pickup. Is that enough to know it\'s packed? Yes. The sentence says an order with that label has been packed. We don\'t need a second fact about its contents.</p>\\r\\n        <p>That\'s a <strong>guarantee</strong>: the rule doesn\'t leave room for a ready order that hasn\'t been packed. It gives us something certain about any order that meets that condition.</p>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"co-role-pair\\"><div><h3>Sufficient means enough</h3><p>Being marked ready for pickup is enough to know the order has been packed. We call it the <strong>sufficient condition</strong>.</p></div><div><h3>Necessary means required</h3><p>An order with that ready label has to have been packed. Packing is required for it. We call it the <strong>necessary condition</strong>.</p></div></div>\\r\\n        <p>These are two jobs in one rule. One condition is enough to establish the other. The other is required whenever the first is true. We\'ll give each job more attention in the next lesson.</p>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"A guarantee is stronger than a tendency\\">\\r\\n        <p>Now compare a guarantee with something that is only usually true.</p>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"co-intro-relationship\\"><div><span>A tendency</span><strong>Orders marked ready for pickup are usually packed.</strong><p>A ready order could be an exception.</p></div><div><span>A conditional rule</span><strong>If an order is marked ready for pickup, it has been packed.</strong><p>Every order with that label has to be packed.</p></div></div>\\r\\n        <p>Usually leaves room for exceptions. A ready order that hasn\'t been packed could fit the first statement. It couldn\'t fit the second.</p>\\r\\n        <p>For an LSAT question, take the stated rule as given. A real shop could make a mistake, but we\'re asking what follows from this statement. We aren\'t checking whether the shop follows its rule in real life.</p>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Use a fact about one order\\">\\r\\n        <blockquote>If an order is marked ready for pickup, it has been packed.</blockquote>\\r\\n        <p>Now add a fact: <strong>Order A is marked ready for pickup.</strong> This is no longer just an imagined case. The question has told us that A meets the condition.</p>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Order A is marked ready for pickup. What do we now know about it?\\">\\r\\n          <p><strong>Order A has been packed.</strong> The rule covers every order with that ready label. The fact tells us A has it. Together, they let us conclude A has been packed.</p>\\r\\n          <p>The rule alone didn\'t tell us A was ready. The separate fact did that. Our conclusion is about A, not every order in the shop.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"The arrow is a shorter way to write it\\">\\r\\n        <p>We can record that relationship with shorter labels. Here, <strong>Marked ready</strong> means marked ready for pickup, and <strong>Packed</strong> means the same order has been packed.</p>\\r\\n        <Arrow left=\\"Marked ready\\" right=\\"Packed\\"/>\\r\\n        <p>The sufficient condition goes on the left: it gives us enough to know the other condition is true. The necessary condition goes on the right: it\'s required whenever the left condition is true.</p>\\r\\n        <p>Read the arrow as <strong>must</strong>: if the order is marked ready for pickup, it must have been packed. It doesn\'t mean “and then,” and it doesn\'t say the label causes packing. This is a connection between what is true, not a timeline.</p>\\r\\n        <p>English doesn\'t always put the sufficient idea first. <strong>An order has been packed if it is marked ready for pickup</strong> expresses the same rule with the ideas in a different order. The ready label still gives us packing, so the diagram stays the same. Meaning decides the two sides.</p>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Change the fact, keep the rule\\">\\r\\n        <p>Keep the rule exactly the same. This time, we\'re told about packing instead of the ready label.</p>\\r\\n        <blockquote>If an order is marked ready for pickup, it has been packed.</blockquote>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Order B has been packed. Do we know whether it is marked ready for pickup?\\">\\r\\n          <p><strong>We don\'t know.</strong> B could have the ready label. It could also be packed without that label. Both possibilities fit the statement.</p>\\r\\n          <p>The rule tells us about orders marked ready for pickup. It hasn\'t said every packed order gets that label. Packing alone doesn\'t answer whether B is ready.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n        <p>In the drawing, orders marked ready sit inside packed orders. Every ready order has to be packed. A packed order could be inside or outside the ready group. Compare the two facts to see what each one tells us.</p>\\r\\n        <SetExplorer/>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Try the same reasoning with a new rule\\">\\r\\n        <p>You used the ready label to establish packing. Starting with packing left the label unknown. Try that distinction with a different sentence.</p>\\r\\n        <Check prompt=\\"Every volunteer wears a badge. Ari wears a badge. Is Ari necessarily a volunteer?\\" options={[\'Yes, the badge proves it.\', \'No, Ari could have a badge for another reason.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'You used the rule backward. Every volunteer has a badge, but the sentence does not say everyone with a badge is a volunteer. A staff member wearing one would fit the rule too.\', \'A badge alone leaves volunteer status unknown. The sentence allows a staff member with a badge; it has not restricted badges to volunteers.\']}/>\\r\\n        <p>A badge may make volunteer status seem plausible. Check whether the sentence actually told you that everyone with a badge is a volunteer. This one didn\'t.</p>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Keep what the sentence actually gives you\\">\\r\\n        <p>Keep the sentence\'s own strength. A rule can give you permission to do something without saying you did it. It can also tell you what you\'re supposed to do without reporting that you followed the instruction. Those are different claims.</p>\\r\\n        <blockquote>Every guest with a ticket may use the cloakroom.</blockquote>\\r\\n        <p>May use gives permission here. A guest with a ticket is allowed to use the cloakroom. That guest could leave their coat on and never go inside. The permission is still there.</p>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Lena is a guest with a ticket. Do we know that she used the cloakroom?\\">\\r\\n          <p>No. We know she\'s allowed to use it because the rule gives that permission to every guest with a ticket. We haven\'t been told whether she used it.</p>\\r\\n          <p>Compare this instruction: <strong>If your coat is wet, hang it on the rack.</strong> A wet coat makes the instruction call for hanging it up. That doesn\'t report anyone carrying out the instruction. We\'d need a fact about what they actually did.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n        <Check prompt=\\"The notice says: If a tray is empty, return it to the counter. This tray is empty. What does the instruction establish?\\" options={[\'The tray has been returned.\', \'The instruction calls for returning the tray.\', \'The tray cannot be returned.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\\r\\n          \\"You turned an instruction into a completed action. The notice tells us what to do with an empty tray; it hasn\'t reported that anyone did it.\\",\\r\\n          \\"The empty tray meets the condition in the instruction, so the notice calls for returning it. Whether someone has returned it is a separate question.\\",\\r\\n          \\"The notice gives an instruction to return the tray. It doesn\'t say returning it is impossible. Keep what the sentence directs separate from what has actually happened.\\",\\r\\n        ]}/>\\r\\n        <p>Before drawing a conclusion, ask what the rule gives you: a fact, permission, or an instruction. Keep that meaning in your answer. Allowed to use isn\'t used, and told to return isn\'t returned.</p>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n    </>}\\r\\n    {roles && <>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Sufficient means enough\\">\\r\\n        <p>Being marked ready for pickup is enough to know an order has been packed. That makes the ready label <strong>sufficient</strong> for packing. Sufficient means enough.</p>\\r\\n        <blockquote>If an order is marked ready for pickup, it has been packed.</blockquote>\\r\\n        <p>The rule already tells you what has to be true of every order with that label. We call being marked ready the <strong>sufficient condition</strong>. Here, sufficient means enough to establish packing under this particular rule.</p>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Order C is marked ready. Do you need another fact about C to know it has been packed?\\">\\r\\n          <p>No. The ready label meets the condition the rule tells us about. The rule and that fact are enough to establish packing.</p>\\r\\n          <p>This doesn\'t make the label the only possible way to find out that an order is packed. It gives us one way to settle that question.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Enough does not mean the only way\\">\\r\\n        <p>Suppose Order D isn\'t marked ready. We no longer have the fact that allowed us to use the rule in its stated direction. But that doesn\'t settle the packing question.</p>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Order D isn\'t marked ready. Could it still have been packed?\\">\\r\\n          <p>Yes. D could be packed without a ready label. It could also be unpacked. Neither possibility creates a ready order that hasn\'t been packed, so both fit the rule.</p>\\r\\n          <p>The sentence gives us one condition that settles packing. It hasn\'t said packing happens only for those orders. When that sufficient condition isn\'t present, the other condition may still be true.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n        <p>Use a new rule to check whether you can recognize what is enough.</p>\\r\\n        <Check prompt=\\"Every delivery marked collected has a pickup receipt. What is sufficient here?\\" options={[\'Marked collected\', \'Has a pickup receipt\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'Marked collected is enough to establish a pickup receipt. The rule tells us what is true of every delivery with that label.\', \'You chose the required result. The sentence gives a receipt to every delivery marked collected; it does not say every delivery with a receipt has that label.\']}/>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Necessary means required\\">\\r\\n        <p>Now look at the other condition in the same rule. An order marked ready for pickup has to have been packed. Packing is required for an order with that label. That makes being packed <strong>necessary</strong> for being marked ready.</p>\\r\\n        <p>We call being packed the <strong>necessary condition</strong>. Necessary means required. It names something that has to be true whenever the sufficient condition is true.</p>\\r\\n        <p>Ask “required for what?” Here, required for an order marked ready. The relationship gives the word its meaning.</p>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Which condition does a ready order have to meet?\\">\\r\\n          <p>It has to be packed. Otherwise we\'d have a ready order that wasn\'t packed, which the sentence rules out.</p>\\r\\n          <p>The ready label is enough to establish packing, and packing is required for every ready order. Those are two views of the same relationship.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"co-role-pair\\"><div><h3>Sufficient</h3><p>Marked ready: enough to establish packing.</p><strong>Goes left</strong></div><div><h3>Necessary</h3><p>Packed: required for every ready order.</p><strong>Goes right</strong></div></div>\\r\\n        <p>Now compare what each starting fact tells us. Keep the same rule while you switch between the ready label and packing.</p>\\r\\n        <GateExplorer/>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Having a requirement does not guarantee the result\\">\\r\\n        <p>Let\'s use a different requirement.</p>\\r\\n        <blockquote>Entering the archive requires a pass.</blockquote>\\r\\n        <p>The sentence tells us what someone needs for entry: a pass. If someone enters the archive, they have that pass. That\'s why has a pass belongs on the required side.</p>\\r\\n        <Arrow left=\\"Enters the archive\\" right=\\"Has a pass\\"/>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Mina has a pass. Does this sentence establish that she entered the archive?\\">\\r\\n          <p>No. Mina could have a pass and remain outside. The rule tells us what entry requires; it doesn\'t tell us that every person with a pass enters.</p>\\r\\n          <p>Necessary doesn\'t mean enough. A requirement can be present while the other condition remains unknown. To conclude Mina entered, we\'d need information establishing that additional connection.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n        <Check prompt=\\"Every finalist receives an invitation. Which requirement does this sentence establish?\\" options={[\'Receiving an invitation is necessary for being a finalist.\', \'Being a finalist is necessary for receiving an invitation.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'The sentence gives an invitation to every finalist. That makes receiving one required for finalist status; it does not restrict invitations to finalists.\', \\"You reversed the requirement. Your choice would mean anyone receiving an invitation has to be a finalist. The sentence allows someone who isn\'t a finalist to receive an invitation too.\\"]}/>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Try the sentence from the inside\\">\\r\\n        <p>We can check a proposed arrow by imagining a case in which its left side is true. Read the original sentence and ask what you now have to know about that same case. Your answer should match the right side of the arrow.</p>\\r\\n        <p>This is a <strong>Personalized If/Then</strong>. Read the rule as if it concerns you or something of yours. The point is to test what the sentence guarantees, not guess what usually happens.</p>\\r\\n        <blockquote>If an order is marked ready for pickup, it has been packed.</blockquote>\\r\\n        <p>For this rule, imagine an order of yours. Keep the same order in mind on both sides.</p>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"If my order is marked ready, what do I know about it?\\">\\r\\n          <p>It has been packed. Every order marked ready is packed, and my imagined order has that label. Marked ready → Packed matches what the sentence tells me.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"If my order has been packed, must it be marked ready?\\">\\r\\n          <p>No. My order could be packed without a ready label. That fits every ready order is packed because it doesn\'t create a ready order that hasn\'t been packed.</p>\\r\\n          <p>Packed → Marked ready would add a claim about every packed order. The sentence doesn\'t give me that direction. Trying both readings lets me catch the reverse instead of accepting an arrow just because it looks familiar.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <Section title=\\"Read the roles in the relationship\\">\\r\\n        <p>In <strong>Marked ready → Packed</strong>, the left condition is sufficient for the right: it\'s enough to establish it. The right condition is necessary for the left: it\'s required whenever the left holds.</p>\\r\\n        <p>These names describe roles in this rule. A different sentence could give the same idea a different role. Don\'t ask whether a pass is sufficient or necessary by itself. Ask what the complete sentence says having the pass does.</p>\\r\\n        <p>The next two groups give us ways to recognize these roles in varied wording. We\'ll keep returning to the meaning because an indicator can only help if you know what complete idea it refers to.</p>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n    </>}\\r\\n  </>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction GroupLessons({ id }: { id: string }) {\\r\\n  const group = GROUPS.find(item => item.id === (id === \'group-1\' ? \'g1\' : \'g2\'))!;\\r\\n  const first = id === \'group-1\';\\r\\n  return <>\\r\\n    <Section title={first ? \'Find the sufficient idea\' : \'Find what is required\'}>\\r\\n      <p>{first\\r\\n        ? \\"A sufficient condition gives you enough information to establish the other condition. Group 1 helps you recognize that job in several kinds of sentence. We\'ll work through the meaning of each expression, then practice finding its complete target.\\"\\r\\n        : \\"A necessary condition is something the other condition requires. Group 2 helps us recognize what must be true when that other condition holds. The requirement belongs on the right because the left condition cannot hold without it. Having the requirement, though, leaves the left condition unknown unless something else settles it.\\"}</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"co-vocabulary\\">{group.words.map(word => <span key={word}>{word}</span>)}</div>\\r\\n      <p>An <strong>indicator</strong> is an expression that helps us recognize the relationship. Its <strong>target</strong> is the complete idea it refers to. Finding that idea matters more than taking the next few words in the sentence.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Before looking for a word, ask what the sentence says. Does it give a rule, cover every member of a group, promise a result, or name something required? Each can tell us that if one condition holds, another must hold. A sentence about what usually happens leaves room for exceptions; a conditional rule makes its consequence certain whenever its sufficient condition holds.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Read the arrow as <strong>must</strong>. The sufficient condition goes on the left. The necessary condition goes on the right. If the left condition is true, the right condition must be true too. The arrow doesn\'t say which event happened first, and it doesn\'t establish that one event caused the other.</p>\\r\\n    </Section>\\r\\n    <Section title={first ? \'Different wording can make the same rule\' : \'Read it as a requirement\'}>\\r\\n      {first ? <>\\r\\n        <p>Suppose a studio has this rule: every painting with a silver seal has been inspected. Having the seal is enough to establish inspection. Let\'s keep that meaning and change the wording.</p>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"co-word-comparison\\"><div><blockquote>If a painting has a silver seal, it has been inspected.</blockquote><p>If what? It has a silver seal. That complete idea goes on the left.</p></div><div><blockquote>A painting has been inspected whenever it has a silver seal.</blockquote><p>Whenever what? It has a silver seal. The sufficient condition comes later in this sentence, but it still goes on the left.</p></div></div>\\r\\n        <Arrow left=\\"Has silver seal\\" right=\\"Has been inspected\\"/>\\r\\n        <p>The indicator can appear at the beginning or in the middle. Sentence position doesn\'t choose the side of the arrow. Find the idea the expression refers to, then ask what the sentence tells you if that idea is true.</p>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Each painting with a silver seal has been inspected. Did changing every to each change the rule?\\">\\r\\n          <p>No. Each still covers every painting with that seal. A painting with the seal that hadn\'t been inspected would break either statement. Keep has silver seal on the left and has been inspected on the right.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n        <p>Some wording presents a rule: <strong>if, when, whenever</strong>. Some covers a whole group: <strong>all, each, any, every</strong>. Read each in its sentence. Any in “Do you have any paint?” asks a question; it doesn\'t give us a rule.</p>\\r\\n        <p>Other sentences promise an outcome: “A silver seal ensures the painting has been inspected” or “A silver seal implies the painting has been inspected.” Here, the promised outcome is inspection. Ensures and implies express the arrow between the two complete ideas. Leads to, will, and always can also express a definite result in a rule, but the word alone doesn\'t settle the meaning. “The studio will open tomorrow” gives us no sufficient condition to put on the left.</p>\\r\\n        <p>We\'ll now examine the Group 1 expressions individually. Keep asking what each sentence makes sufficient, rather than sorting words without their meaning.</p>\\r\\n      </> : <>\\r\\n        <p>A useful way to read the whole rule is: <strong>the left condition requires the right condition</strong>. Suppose borrowing a studio camera requires a current membership. What is required for borrowing? A current membership. That\'s the necessary condition.</p>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"co-word-comparison\\"><div><blockquote>Borrowing a studio camera requires a current membership.</blockquote><p>The required idea comes after requires. Find the whole idea: a current membership.</p></div><div><blockquote>A current membership is required to borrow a studio camera.</blockquote><p>The same required idea now comes first. Moving it in the sentence hasn\'t changed what borrowing requires.</p></div></div>\\r\\n        <Arrow left=\\"Borrows studio camera\\" right=\\"Has current membership\\"/>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Mina has a current membership. Does this rule tell us she borrowed a camera?\\">\\r\\n          <p>No. Membership is something borrowing requires. Mina could have the membership and never borrow a camera. The rule tells us what we need if she borrows; having what she needs doesn\'t tell us she did.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n        <p>Notice the meaning shared by <strong>requires, necessitates, depends on,</strong> and <strong>relies on</strong> when they express a strict requirement. If borrowing depends on having a current membership, borrowing still requires membership. “Depends partly on” may describe an influence instead, so read the whole claim before treating it as a conditional.</p>\\r\\n        <p>You may also hear the requirement as “In order to borrow a camera, you must have a current membership.” The goal is borrowing; the required condition is membership. Only and only if can set the same restriction. We\'ll work through their wording next.</p>\\r\\n        <Check prompt=\\"Using the recording booth depends on having a reservation. What belongs on the right?\\" options={[\'Uses recording booth\', \'Has a reservation\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'Using the booth is what needs the reservation. Putting use on the right would make a reservation enough to establish that someone used the booth, which the sentence never says.\', \'A reservation is required for using the booth, so it belongs on the right. Having a reservation still leaves open whether the person uses it.\']}/>\\r\\n        <p>You won\'t always see a familiar word. Find what the sentence says is required <strong>for the other condition</strong>. Then check that your arrow keeps that requirement on the right.</p>\\r\\n      </>}\\r\\n    </Section>\\r\\n    <IndicatorSections id={id}/>\\r\\n    <Section title={first ? \'Find the target, then place it\' : \'Find the requirement, then place it\'}>\\r\\n      <p>{first\\r\\n        ? \\"Add what to the indicator when that gives you a sensible question. If what? All what? The only what? Your answer should be the whole idea the expression refers to. Then check whether that idea really is enough to establish the other condition.\\"\\r\\n        : \\"Ask what the indicator refers to. Only what? Only if what? What is required? The target can come before or after the expression, so check its meaning in the complete sentence.\\"}</p>\\r\\n      <p>This is the <strong>What Test</strong>. The question helps you find the indicator\'s complete target before choosing its side of the arrow. Keep any words that limit which people, objects, places, or occasions the sentence covers. The question finds the idea; the whole sentence tells you what that idea does.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Work through the expressions below. First choose the complete target. Then place it on its side of the arrow and read the relationship in ordinary English.</p>\\r\\n      <TranslationLab id={id}/>\\r\\n    </Section>\\r\\n    <Section title=\\"Keep the whole condition\\" dark>\\r\\n      <blockquote>{first ? \'Any applicant who submits late pays a fee.\' : \'Entry requires a current pass.\'}</blockquote>\\r\\n      <p>{first\\r\\n        ? \\"Applicant alone isn\'t the condition. The sentence is about an applicant who submits late. Keep that restriction when you shorten the idea; otherwise your diagram would make a claim about on-time applicants too.\\"\\r\\n        : \\"A current pass is required. Has a pass drops current and would include an expired pass. Shortening a label should save writing while preserving what the sentence requires.\\"}</p>\\r\\n      <Check prompt={first ? \'What goes left in this rule?\' : \'What goes right in this rule?\'} options={first ? [\'Applicant\', \'Applicant submits late\'] : [\'Has current pass\', \'Has any pass\']} correct={first ? 1 : 0} feedback={first\\r\\n        ? [\'You dropped the late-submission restriction. Applicant alone would cover every applicant, including someone who submits on time. The sufficient idea is applicant submits late.\', \'This keeps the complete sufficient idea. The rule covers applicants who submit late, so keep that restriction with the applicant.\']\\r\\n        : [\'This keeps the full requirement. Entry needs a current pass; an expired pass does not meet that requirement.\', \'You dropped current from the requirement. Has any pass would include an expired pass, which is not what the sentence requires.\']}/>\\r\\n    </Section>\\r\\n    <Section title={first ? \'Read the only as a complete expression\' : \'Compare only with the only\'}>\\r\\n      {first ? <>\\r\\n        <blockquote>The only people admitted are members.</blockquote>\\r\\n        <p>The only what? The only people admitted. The complete target is admitted people. If someone is admitted, the sentence tells us they\'re a member.</p>\\r\\n        <Arrow left=\\"Admitted\\" right=\\"Member\\"/>\\r\\n        <p>A member who stays outside fits this rule. Nothing says every member is admitted. Check that your diagram keeps that possibility open.</p>\\r\\n        <Check prompt=\\"The only notebooks kept on this shelf are hardback. Which diagram preserves the rule?\\" options={[\'Hardback → Kept on shelf\', \'Kept on shelf → Hardback\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'You made being hardback enough for a place on the shelf. The sentence limits the notebooks kept there; it does not put every hardback notebook on this shelf.\', \'A notebook kept on this shelf has to be hardback. A hardback notebook on another shelf would also fit the rule, so this direction keeps what the sentence actually says.\']}/>\\r\\n      </> : <>\\r\\n        <p>Try the distinction on the order rule we already understand. The wording changes, but a ready label still tells us the order has been packed.</p>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"co-word-comparison\\"><div><blockquote>Only packed orders are marked ready.</blockquote><p>Only refers to packed orders. Packing is required for the ready label, so packed goes right.</p></div><div><blockquote>The only orders marked ready are packed orders.</blockquote><p>The only refers to orders marked ready. That label is enough to establish packing, so marked ready goes left.</p></div></div>\\r\\n        <Arrow left=\\"Marked ready\\" right=\\"Packed\\"/>\\r\\n        <p>Both sentences preserve the same direction. An order that is packed but not marked ready fits both. Neither sentence makes packing alone enough for the label.</p>\\r\\n        <Check prompt=\\"Only registered guests receive wristbands. What follows from receiving a wristband?\\" options={[\'The person is a registered guest.\', \'Nothing about registration.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'Only limits wristbands to registered guests, so receiving one establishes that the person is registered.\', \'You treated the sentence like all registered guests receive wristbands. Only restricts who receives one, so the wristband does establish that the person is a registered guest.\']}/>\\r\\n      </>}\\r\\n    </Section>\\r\\n    <Section title=\\"From sentence to diagram\\">\\r\\n      <p>You have seen the expressions with help. Now use a new sentence. Identify both complete ideas, choose the sufficient one for the left, and check whether your diagram says what the sentence says.</p>\\r\\n      <p>If you know the meaning but hesitate over the arrow, imagine the left condition is true. Does the sentence then require the right condition? Read the whole relationship in English. If it makes a promise the original didn\'t make, change the direction.</p>\\r\\n      <DiagramBuilder id={id}/>\\r\\n      <details className=\\"co-practical-note\\"><summary>Why write a diagram when I understand the sentence?</summary><p>For one short sentence, you may be able to hold the connection in your head. Here, writing it makes your direction and complete conditions visible so you can check them. If your first diagram doesn\'t match the meaning, find the exact phrase you misread and revise that part.</p></details>\\r\\n    </Section>\\r\\n    <Section title=\\"Say the rule without the scaffold\\">\\r\\n      <p>Read the new sentence and explain its direction before revealing. If you hesitate, ask what the indicator refers to, then try the proposed relationship in ordinary English. Compare your explanation with the one that appears.</p>\\r\\n      <Flashcards id={id}/>\\r\\n    </Section>\\r\\n    <Section title=\\"Check the meaning, not just the word\\">\\r\\n      <Check prompt={first ? \'A report is reviewed if submitted before noon. Which is the same rule?\' : \'A student graduates only if the project is completed. Which is the same rule?\'} options={first ? [\'If reviewed, it was submitted before noon.\', \'If submitted before noon, it is reviewed.\'] : [\'If the student graduates, the project was completed.\', \'If the project is completed, the student graduates.\']} correct={first ? 1 : 0} feedback={first\\r\\n        ? [\'You reversed the if relationship. Submission before noon is enough for review; the sentence has not said review proves when the report was submitted.\', \'This preserves the if-clause as the sufficient condition. Submission before noon gives us review even though it appears second in the original sentence.\']\\r\\n        : [\'This preserves project completion as a requirement for graduation. It does not turn completing the project into a promise of graduation.\', \'You turned the only-if requirement into a guarantee. Graduation requires completion, but the sentence allows a completed project without graduation.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>The guided practice asks you to write your reasoning with the method beside you. Then the attached drill gives you fresh questions. Use the explanation to inspect the direction and complete conditions, not only whether you chose the same answer.</p>\\r\\n    </Section>\\r\\n  </>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction OpeningFigure({ unitId }: { unitId: string }) {\\r\\n  if (unitId === \'orientation\') return <figure className=\\"co-hero-figure co-meaning-figure\\">\\r\\n    <p className=\\"co-kicker\\">What follows if a condition is true</p>\\r\\n    <p className=\\"co-hero-sentence\\">What would we know <strong>if</strong> this were true?</p>\\r\\n    <div className=\\"co-hypothetical-tag\\">A situation to imagine</div>\\r\\n    <figcaption>A conditional tells us what must be true if the first condition is true. It doesn\'t tell us that the first condition actually is true.</figcaption>\\r\\n  </figure>;\\r\\n  if (unitId === \'sufficient-necessary\') return <figure className=\\"co-hero-figure co-roles-figure\\">\\r\\n    <p className=\\"co-kicker\\">Two views of one rule</p>\\r\\n    <p className=\\"co-hero-rule\\">If an order is marked ready for pickup, it has been packed.</p>\\r\\n    <div className=\\"co-role-compass\\"><div><span>Enough</span><strong>Marked ready</strong><small>Gives us packing</small></div><div><span>Required</span><strong>Packed</strong><small>Every ready order needs it</small></div></div>\\r\\n    <figcaption>One condition is enough. The other is required by that same rule.</figcaption>\\r\\n  </figure>;\\r\\n  if (unitId === \'group-1\') return <figure className=\\"co-hero-figure co-sufficient-figure\\">\\r\\n    <p className=\\"co-kicker\\">Read the complete idea</p>\\r\\n    <p className=\\"co-hero-sentence\\">A report is reviewed <mark>if</mark> <strong>it is submitted before noon.</strong></p>\\r\\n    <div className=\\"co-hero-target\\"><span>What is enough for review?</span><strong>Submission before noon</strong></div>\\r\\n    <figcaption>The sufficient condition can come last in the sentence.</figcaption>\\r\\n  </figure>;\\r\\n  return <figure className=\\"co-hero-figure co-required-figure\\">\\r\\n    <p className=\\"co-kicker\\">Read what the sentence needs</p>\\r\\n    <p className=\\"co-hero-sentence\\">Entry requires a <strong>current pass.</strong></p>\\r\\n    <div className=\\"co-pass-figure\\"><span>Required for entry</span><strong>A current pass</strong><small>An expired pass won\'t meet this requirement.</small></div>\\r\\n    <figcaption>Having the pass alone doesn\'t establish entry.</figcaption>\\r\\n  </figure>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nexport function ConditionalOpeningLesson({ unit, onComplete, continueHref, continueLabel = \'Continue to guided practice\', previousHref, reviewed }: ConditionalLessonNoteProps) {\\r\\n  const group = unit.id === \'group-1\' || unit.id === \'group-2\';\\r\\n  const orientation = unit.id === \'orientation\';\\r\\n  const title = group ? unit.id === \'group-1\' ? \'Group 1: what is enough?\' : \'Group 2: what is required?\' : orientation ? \'What Are Conditionals?\' : \'What is enough? What is required?\';\\r\\n  const repairTitle = orientation ? \\"Don\'t turn a rule into a case fact\\" : unit.id === \'sufficient-necessary\' ? \\"Don\'t turn a requirement into a guarantee\\" : unit.id === \'group-1\' ? \'Keep the direction and the whole condition\' : \'Keep requirements and completed actions distinct\';\\r\\n  const subtitle = orientation\\r\\n    ? \\"A conditional tells us that if one thing is true, something else has to be true too. Let\'s see what we can conclude from a rule, and what we still don\'t know.\\"\\r\\n    : group ? unit.id === \'group-1\'\\r\\n      ? \'These expressions can point to the sufficient idea. Read what each one says before deciding which complete condition belongs on the left.\'\\r\\n      : \'These expressions can identify a requirement. Find the complete idea the sentence says you need, then check what its presence does and does not prove.\'\\r\\n    : \\"The same rule gives its two conditions different jobs. Let\'s take each one seriously before giving it a place in the diagram.\\";\\r\\n  return <div className=\\"conditional-note co-opening\\">\\r\\n    <header className={\'co-hero \' + (orientation ? \'co-intro-hero\' : \'\')}>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"co-hero-copy\\"><p className=\\"co-kicker\\">Conditional logic</p><h1>{title}</h1><p>{subtitle}</p>\\r\\n      <a href=\\"#co-reading\\">{orientation ? \'Start with the meaning\' : \'Begin reading\'} <span aria-hidden=\\"true\\">↓</span></a></div>\\r\\n      <OpeningFigure unitId={unit.id}/>\\r\\n    </header>\\r\\n    <div className=\\"co-lesson-navigation\\"><DynamicIslandTOC key={unit.id} selector=\\".co-opening [data-toc]\\" variant=\\"inline\\"/></div>\\r\\n    <article id=\\"co-reading\\">\\r\\n      {orientation ? <ConditionalReferenceSequence/> : group ? <GroupLessons id={unit.id}/> : <Fundamentals roles={unit.id === \'sufficient-necessary\'}/>}\\r\\n      <ConditionalOpeningMedia unitId={unit.id}/>\\r\\n      <Section id=\\"repair\\" title={repairTitle}>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"co-word-comparison\\"><div><h3>The tempting move</h3><p>{unit.commonMistake.mistake}</p></div><div><h3>Read the sentence again</h3><p>{unit.commonMistake.repair}</p></div></div>\\r\\n      </Section>\\r\\n      <footer className=\\"co-footer\\">\\r\\n        <p>{reviewed ? \'You marked this lesson as read. You can return to the examples whenever you need.\' : \'Marking this lesson as read records review. Your practice gives you a chance to use the reasoning yourself.\'}</p>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"co-choices\\">{previousHref && <Link to={previousHref}>Previous lesson</Link>}<button type=\\"button\\" onClick={onComplete}>{reviewed ? \'Lesson read\' : \'Mark lesson as read\'}</button><Link className=\\"co-primary\\" to={continueHref}>{continueLabel} <span aria-hidden=\\"true\\">→</span></Link></div>\\r\\n      </footer>\\r\\n    </article>\\r\\n  </div>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n"}'}]

Our Group 1/2 practice needs broader expression coverage and reasoned feedback; the source\'s basic set alone would not establish that coverage.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What to carry into the Conditional Bootcamp\\r\\n\\r\\n**Joshua\'s instruction on 2026-10-03 changes the conditional curriculum scope and sequencing.** The complete supplied HTML now sets its content-order backbone, as well as its voice: if/then meaning; sufficient and its word family; necessary and its word family; conceptual contrapositive; four situations; diagramming and symbolic contraposition; practical FAQ; indicator targets; Personalized If/Then; integrated basic practice. The [complete ordered skeleton and integration map](../brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/2026-10-02-opening-lessons-source-map.md) is the current authoring plan.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis explicitly includes a conceptual contrapositive before notation and supersedes the earlier restriction to the first four opening units. Existing code does not become sequence-compliant by being linked to this plan. Keep the source\'s logical simplifications bounded, preserve Joshua\'s five-step method and contextual group definitions, and preserve assignment and historical-answer compatibility when implementing the sequence. This source-specific curriculum order does not impose conditional topics on unrelated LSAT lessons.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following rows record the earlier opening-only planning model and useful concept/practice coverage. Their arrangement is **not the current teaching sequence**. Reuse their material in the new ordered skeleton rather than retaining their old lesson order.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Part of our opening | What the learner should understand | Natural teaching progression | Nearby practice |\\r\\n|---|---|---|---|\\r\\n| **What a conditional says** | A statement makes one condition enough to require another. It does not establish that either condition occurs. | Plain definition, purpose, one stated rule, one case, one tempting reverse. | Decide what the given rule and fact establish; explain the limit. |\\r\\n| **Why it matters on the LSAT** | A conclusion can rely on the direction of a rule or on a missing connection. Reversing a relationship can support the wrong answer. | Keep the beginner example; show one supported conclusion and one unsupported inference. | Choose the justified conclusion and name the connection the other answer would require. |\\r\\n| **Sufficient** | Enough to establish the necessary condition under this rule; not the only possible way unless stated. | Same anchor, “enough for what?”, present-case explanation, absence leaves the other condition open. | Find the complete sufficient idea and say what it establishes. |\\r\\n| **Necessary** | Required for the sufficient condition; presence alone does not establish the sufficient condition. | Same anchor, identify what must be there, compare requirement with guarantee. | Identify the requirement; reject an unsupported reverse with a reason. |\\r\\n| **Translation and diagramming** | The diagram preserves the whole relationship, including conditions and qualifications. | Ordinary meaning, indicator, complete ideas, placement, English readback. Introduce later operations when their prerequisites are taught. | Construct a diagram in meaningful steps and compare it with the whole sentence. |\\r\\n| **Group 1** | Joshua\'s Group 1 expressions identify the sufficient idea; sentence order can vary. | Teach a simple expression first, reuse meaning across variants, then alter position and scope. | Lesson, guided translation, fresh independent items, explained feedback. |\\r\\n| **Group 2** | Joshua\'s Group 2 expressions identify the necessary idea; target and force must be read in context. | Teach the requirement first, compare “if” with “only if,” then develop each expression\'s target and nuances. | Separate Group 2 practice, then a controlled Group 1/2 comparison when both are learned. |\\r\\n\\r\\nThese are curriculum planning rows. Student-facing headings should teach the actual concept, such as **What does this sentence require?** They should not expose “Joshua\'s assigned starting stage,” internal sequencing metadata, or a difficulty selector. Joshua assigns the appropriate material; the learner works through that assigned lesson and its practice.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Give an idea several teachable moments\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source rarely handles a significant concept with one definition and one answer. It may need a literal explanation, a familiar example, a variation, a pause, a mistaken interpretation, a correction, and a short practice task.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor Group 1, that could become several small lessons: recognizing “if,” locating the complete if-clause, reading an if-clause at the end of the sentence, handling a universal expression, and checking that the diagram preserves the meaning. Beginner, medium, and advanced describe teacher-assigned work; optional timing belongs to medium and advanced practice after accuracy is established.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Preserve the real indicator groups\\r\\n\\r\\nThe current reviewed opening materials use:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Group 1:** if, when, where, all, the only, every, any.\\r\\n- **Group 2:** only, only if, only when, only where, always, requires, must.\\r\\n\\r\\nSee the [reviewed opening source constraints](../brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/notebooklm-opening-assets/sufficient-necessary-infographic-prompt.txt). The only people admitted are members means **Admitted → Member**. Only members are admitted means the same relationship, reached through a different expression. The lesson must show the meaning rather than encourage a next-word shortcut.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Preserve Joshua\'s five steps\\r\\n\\r\\nIn [Sandra\'s 2026-09-28 transcript](../students/sandra/transcript-downloads/2026-09-28-sandra-notes-by-gemini.md), at 00:43:22, Joshua gives this sequence: identify the indicator; label the two ideas; apply the left/right rule; find the contrapositive; say it back in English. Keep English readback visible as a meaning check throughout.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Carry these improvements forward\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Define before demonstrating.** Start by explaining what a conditional says. Let the example make the definition concrete.\\r\\n2. **Explain the purpose through a decision.** Show how direction changes the conclusion the learner may draw. Avoid unsupported prevalence statistics.\\r\\n3. **Keep one relationship stable while changing the view.** Ordinary sentence, case fact, roles, wording variation, and diagram should fit together.\\r\\n4. **Make each pause a useful thinking task.** Ask for a prediction or explanation, then reveal the reason.\\r\\n5. **Show a mistake being detected.** A wrong arrow becomes understandable when its English meaning fails the original sentence.\\r\\n6. **Teach the target before the placement shortcut becomes a habit.** Complete ideas and their qualifications matter.\\r\\n7. **Explain why the drill exists.** The learner should know what ability they are practicing.\\r\\n8. **Use fresh practice.** Worked examples teach the method; new items show whether the method transfers.\\r\\n9. **Give practical objections an answer.** Time, confidence, notation, and when to write deserve specific guidance.\\r\\n10. **Keep each operation behind its prerequisites.** Under the 2026-10-03 sequence, conceptual contraposition follows both condition roles and families, and precedes notation. Chains, Groups 3/4 and quantities still receive later development. The source does not contain those complete later curricula.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Accuracy and method boundaries\\r\\n\\r\\nWriting that sounds like the source must still preserve correct logic and Joshua\'s chosen method.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Source simplification or context | Boundary for our material |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| “Ignore the conditional” when sufficient is absent or necessary is present. | For this one rule and fact, no new conclusion about the other condition follows. The rule remains available for later facts and chains. Never teach that it disappears. |\\r\\n| Necessary has to happen “at some point.” | A conditional is not necessarily a time sequence or causal claim. Prefer “has to be true if the sufficient condition is true.” |\\r\\n| The original and contrapositive are “all you know.” | The central warning is against an unsupported reverse or inverse. State the immediate inference limits precisely. |\\r\\n| Required words are described as obligations. | Preserve modality. “Interviewees must bring ID” can assert an obligation, not prove compliance. Diagram the stated requirement unless the facts establish compliance. |\\r\\n| Indicator usually comes before target. | Read its full grammatical target. Keep negation, scope, qualifiers, and readability. A short label that loses meaning is not an improvement. |\\r\\n| Try a personalized sufficient guess. | Compare with the whole ordinary meaning and look for a counterexample. A feeling that an arrow is plausible is not enough. |\\r\\n| Original and contrapositive training. | Explain why a drill requires explicit work and when test-day practice may differ. It is not a universal instruction to place the next word on the right. |\\r\\n| Confidence guarantees the diagram is correct. | Confidence can grow from practice, but correctness rests on preserving meaning and valid reasoning. Provide checks. |\\r\\n| Timing and learning claims are absolute. | Treat them as the author\'s advice unless independently supported. Do not import obsolete or unavailable context. |\\r\\n| A theme makes a drill memorable. | Keep each sentence logically interpretable and its answer reviewed. Novelty must not obscure the condition or require untaught knowledge. |\\r\\n\\r\\nFor the parcel example, three possible cases distinguish the permitted relationship from an invalid reverse:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Blue sticker and inspected: fits the rule.\\r\\n- Inspected without a blue sticker: also fits the rule.\\r\\n- Blue sticker without inspection: breaks the rule.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe rule does not itself say any such parcel exists. Examples of possible cases illustrate consistency, not existence claims. This distinction matters when moving from individual facts to general rules.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Calibration examples for different LSAT surfaces\\r\\n\\r\\nAll examples below are original drafts for this reference. They demonstrate writing mechanisms; they are not assigned work or approved curriculum.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Explain sufficient and necessary without rushing\\r\\n\\r\\n> Every parcel with a blue sticker has been inspected.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Suppose yours has a blue sticker. That\'s enough to know it has been inspected. You don\'t need another fact about the parcel. The rule has already told you what must be true of every parcel with that sticker.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We call the blue sticker the **sufficient condition**. Sufficient means enough. Here, enough to establish inspection under this rule.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Inspection is the **necessary condition**. A blue-sticker parcel has to meet that requirement. Otherwise it would be an exception to a rule that allows no exceptions.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Now suppose a parcel has been inspected. Does it have to have a blue sticker?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We still don\'t know. Inspection was required for the blue-sticker parcels. The shop never said those were the only parcels it inspected.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis returns to meaning at every term. The example does not assert why the shop uses stickers or when they are applied. Those extra facts are unnecessary.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Teach a necessary expression through its whole meaning\\r\\n\\r\\n> Editing this newsletter requires an account.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> What does the sentence say the editor needs? An account. Keep that complete idea on the required side of the relationship:\\r\\n>\\r\\n> **Edits this newsletter → Has an account**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Read it back: if someone edits this newsletter, they have an account. That matches the sentence.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Try the reverse. If someone has an account, do they necessarily edit the newsletter? The sentence hasn\'t told us that. An account could belong to someone who only reads it.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe final possible counterexample is introduced as something consistent with the sentence, not an asserted fact about this system. Technical placement has a semantic reason.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Give a flashcard a reasoning task\\r\\n\\r\\n**Front**\\r\\n\\r\\n> Every package in Locker 4 has been scanned. A package has been scanned. Must it be in Locker 4? Why?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Back**\\r\\n\\r\\n> No. The rule tells us about packages already in Locker 4. It doesn\'t say every scanned package goes there.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is more useful than a card that only asks “Necessary condition = which side?” Keep simple recall cards when recall is the actual skill; do not mistake that for complete reasoning practice.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Make feedback identify the missed connection\\r\\n\\r\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"0713b8","wall_time_seconds":5.4778521,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3793,"output":"      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      title: \'Requires: the target can come before the word\',\\r\\n      paragraphs: [\\r\\n        \\"What does entry require? Required to attend interview is longer than attends interview, but here those extra words are doing necessary work.\\",\\r\\n      ],\\r\\n    },\\r\\n  ],\\r\\n};\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction IndicatorSections({ id }: { id: string }) {\\r\\n  return <>{indicatorExplanations[id].map((lesson, index) => {\\r\\n    const item = translationExamples[id][index];\\r\\n    return <Section key={item.word} title={lesson.title} expressionNumber={index + 1}>\\r\\n      <blockquote>{item.sentence}</blockquote>\\r\\n      {lesson.paragraphs.map(paragraph => <p key={paragraph}>{paragraph}</p>)}\\r\\n      {id === \'group-2\' && item.word === \'only if\' && <>\\r\\n        <p>Try reading the sentence as though it concerns you. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 7.1 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"86618c","wall_time_seconds":3.5253601,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":6410,"output":"6. Show the diagram after its meaning is understood.\\r\\n\\r\\nIntroduce a fresh example for independent practice. The learner should not be able to answer only because the lesson already solved that sentence.\\r\\n\\r\\nA repeated “Keep this” slogan without new reasoning is not explanatory repetition. Nor is rendering the same instructions twice in different panels. See the demonstrated corrections in [COPY-CORRECTIONS](../wiki/COPY-CORRECTIONS.md).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Metaphor gives the reader a usable handle\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source uses doors, families, activation, burdens, brackets, and putting yourself in a condition\'s shoes. Each metaphor gives an abstract operation a physical or social handle. A small set of terms recurs, so the reader can keep using it.\\r\\n\\r\\nTransfer the method of choosing a metaphor, not the particular inventory. Prefer a familiar image that helps answer a logical question. Explain its literal meaning immediately. Remove it when it adds more things to remember than it clarifies.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor instance, a ticket can illustrate a requirement only if the rule is stated carefully. “A ticket is required to enter” does not say a ticket guarantees entry. An analogy fails if it smuggles in that reverse.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not build a competing metaphor for every sentence. Do not invent branded names for every skill. The standard technical terms remain the stable vocabulary.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Humor reduces tension without changing the rule\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source\'s coffee obsession makes an unusual absolute rule memorable. Its reluctant-student aside acknowledges the experience of being asked to guess. The imagined green checkmark gives the reader\'s desire for certainty a recognizable shape.\\r\\n\\r\\nHumor can occur inside an explanation when it makes the thought easier to understand. Joshua\'s source selection supersedes the earlier blanket restriction that wit must stay outside the explanation. It does not authorize mockery, forced slang, exaggerated praise, or an expanding comic story.\\r\\n\\r\\nUse a light aside only when it helps the reader inhabit a situation or relax around a specific mistake. Keep it optional. A paragraph should still teach clearly if the aside is removed. Do not use the source\'s distinctive jokes as templates to be copied.\\r\\n\\r\\nNever turn first-person source anecdotes into Joshua\'s biography. “I ask every student this” requires that Joshua actually does. “Students always learn better this way” requires evidence or a narrower, truthful statement.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Emphasis and visuals identify the decision\\r\\n\\r\\nBold in the source often marks the rule, an inference, a warning, or an instruction. Italics distinguish examples and sometimes emphasize a word that changes the contrast. A table lets the reader compare controlled variations. A STOP asks the reader to attempt something. A side note answers a local question without interrupting the main line for everyone.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor our material:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Bold the relationship or phrase that controls the next decision. Do not bold most of a paragraph.\\r\\n- Give an example its own space. The student should be able to find the sentence currently under discussion.\\r\\n- Put comparisons side by side when the same rule or wording is being contrasted.\\r\\n- Reveal diagram construction one meaningful step at a time. Explain each placement in English.\\r\\n- Preserve a readable text equivalent for every visual. The illustration is an explanation, not a substitute for one.\\r\\n- Make an interactive pause real. Let the learner choose when to reveal the reasoning.\\r\\n- Give a side note a specific job: answer a question, define new notation, or qualify advice. Avoid a second full lesson in a callout.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua\'s notation correction still applies: teaching arrows should look like teaching notation, not little implementation-code boxes. Clear ordinary typography and meaningful labels should communicate the relationship.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source\'s adjusted HTML design is not a visual brand template. Our bootcamp should preserve the established Intro to LR student flow while using original visuals that serve the current concept. Student pages show the assigned work and the lesson itself; internal stage planning, assigned-start metadata, production notes, and selectable difficulty controls do not belong in the teaching prose.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The complete source progression and depth\\r\\n\\r\\nThis map records what the supplied excerpt does in order. It is not an assertion that every future lesson should cover every listed topic.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. The relationship comes before its parts\\r\\n\\r\\n**The Art of the If/Then**, HTML lines 142 to 154, opens with a plain definition, a single familiar rule, a literal interpretation, several statements of certainty, and a reason to understand the relationship beneath varied language. The transition promises to take the same example apart.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe depth comes from making “must” meaningful before presenting a list of words. The reader learns what kind of relationship they are looking for. The source also connects certainty to prior “Power Players” material, which is not included in this attachment. Our standalone introduction must supply any needed context itself.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** first explain what a conditional says and why its direction matters. Then give a concrete example. Do not open with a diagramming task or make the definition a label attached after a quiz.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Sufficient is explained through presence and absence\\r\\n\\r\\n**The Sufficient Condition**, lines 156 to 199, contains a definition, the recurring anchor, a metaphor, the possibility that the sufficient condition does not occur, a contrast between its absence and presence, and a clarification of “activation.” It then shows **eight indicator rows with eleven displayed example forms**, all expressing the same anchor relationship, and explains why language recognition cannot replace understanding.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is more than “sufficient goes left.” The text develops what the condition does, what it does not establish, and how wording changes around it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** give sufficient its own explanation, contrasting cases, and nearby practice. A left-side label is useful only after “enough for what?” has a clear answer.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Necessary is developed as a requirement\\r\\n\\r\\n**The Necessary Condition**, lines 201 to 230, defines the other part, reuses the same rule, explains the requirement, and shows **ten indicator rows with eleven displayed forms**. It compares the varied wording with the sufficient-family statements and gives special attention to “only if.” It ends by explaining why symbols help isolate the relationship.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source uses the ordinary force of “necessary,” “required,” and “need” to make the technical term familiar. It does not jump directly to a memorized side rule.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** explain what is required and why having a requirement is not the same as satisfying every condition for the result. Teach “if” and “only if” using a controlled comparison. Keep the target of each expression clear.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 4. The contrapositive is discovered before it is manipulated\\r\\n\\r\\n**The Contrapositive**, lines 234 to 285, first recovers the original relationship. It introduces a new coffee/walking thought experiment, removes the required condition, asks for a prediction, and explicitly pauses. The answer is derived from the unmet requirement. The term is then named, the original anchor revisited, and a four-situation chart sets limits on inference.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe order is important: meaning, prediction, reason, name, comparison. The flip-and-negate shortcut appears later, after the reader has a reason to believe the result.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** preserve this order when contraposition is actually in scope. Do not rush the full procedure into the opening definition merely because it appears early in this source.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 5. Notation is introduced as a solution to varied wording\\r\\n\\r\\n**How to Diagram Conditionals**, lines 289 to 388, recovers the indicator families, explains the arrow, gives a four-step construction procedure, and builds one diagram in stages. It then explains negation, displays four original/contrapositive sign patterns, gives the shortcut, and distinguishes writing a contrapositive from reading one when needed.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe first diagram is narrated: notice the indicator, place its target, then complete the other side. Its final appearance is not used as evidence that the learner understands how to make it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Transfer:** show each operation and its reason. Preserve Joshua\'s method and meaningful labels rather than copying the source\'s four-step count or abbreviation rule.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 6. Practical objections receive substantial answers\\r\\n\\r\\n> You used the sentence in the reverse direction. “Only registered visitors enter the archive” requires registration for entry. It hasn\'t said every registered visitor enters. Read the diagram as **Enters → Registered** and compare it with the sentence.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe feedback names the mistake, shows the relevant meaning, and gives a repair. It avoids generic praise, mockery, and labels such as “weak reasoning.”\\r\\n\\r\\n### Explain an ordinary learning objection\\r\\n\\r\\n> “I understood the sentence. Why write it down?”\\r\\n>\\r\\n> With one short rule, you may not need to. When a passage gives you several relationships, a diagram lets you compare them without rereading the wording each time. In this exercise, write the relationship so we can check that you kept its direction and complete ideas.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe answer gives a decision criterion and distinguishes the purpose of this exercise from a blanket rule about every test question.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Transfer the voice to another LSAT topic\\r\\n\\r\\n> A conclusion is the claim the author is asking you to accept. The other statements are supposed to support it.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Nora says, “The library should stay open later because every evening seat was taken this week.” What is she trying to persuade us of?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> That the library should stay open later. The full seats are her reason. She expects that reason to support the proposed change.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> You don\'t have to agree with her. First, separate what she wants you to accept from what she gives you in support.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe same mechanism works outside conditionals: definition, small example, question, explanation, and a useful boundary. No conditional topic has been imported into the conclusion lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Revise the draft in a useful order\\r\\n\\r\\n### First, check the reasoning and scope\\r\\n\\r\\nList what is given, what follows, and why. Try to construct a case that satisfies the given information but makes the proposed conclusion false. If that case is possible, revise the logic before polishing the voice. Check modality, negation, quantifier scope, and whether the learner has actually been taught every required operation.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor a rewrite, preserve Joshua\'s established method and explicit lesson scope. The new reference governs delivery. It does not authorize removing content that students need or adding source topics the current assignment does not cover.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Then, check the learner\'s experience\\r\\n\\r\\nRead as someone who has never seen the notation. Can they tell what the concept is? Can they answer the first question with what the page has taught? Does each new term refer to an idea they have seen? Does the page tell them why the correct answer follows?\\r\\n\\r\\nPut the explanation beside the point where it is needed. Do not rely on an interaction to imply a distinction the prose never explains. A student who cannot use the animation must still be able to learn from the text.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Then, listen to the voice\\r\\n\\r\\nRead aloud at an ordinary teaching pace. Replace stiff phrasing with the words the teacher would naturally use. Keep the intermediate thoughts. Vary sentence length where the task changes. Remove repeated catchphrases, inflated enthusiasm, branded metaphors, and irrelevant asides.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not repair generic prose by scattering “Cool,” “Let\'s,” or “That\'s it” through it. Repair the missing reasoning, the abrupt transition, or the abstract example.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Finally, verify the student surface\\r\\n\\r\\nCheck the actual prompt, answer state, labels, buttons, diagrams, and explanations. A good note can be undermined by a shell that exposes internal planning or reveals the answer too soon. Preview desktop and mobile when the interface changes. Keep the instructor\'s planning map separate from what the learner sees.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Use this rubric before handing over LSAT writing\\r\\n\\r\\nScore each dimension from 0 to 2: **0** absent or misleading; **1** partly present but needing revision; **2** clear and usable. This is an editorial tool, not a validated learning measure. A logical error or scope violation requires revision regardless of the total.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Dimension | What a strong draft does |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| **Ordinary meaning** | Defines the idea in language the reader can understand before notation. |\\r\\n| **Concrete anchor** | Uses an original, small, unambiguous situation and states needed assumptions. |\\r\\n| **Visible reasoning** | Shows the intermediate connection instead of asserting a result. |\\r\\n| **Point of view** | Keeps the reader involved; uses teacher narration purposefully. |\\r\\n| **Cadence** | Gives complex thoughts room and short conclusions a clear place to land. |\\r\\n| **Vocabulary** | Keeps useful technical terms, explains them, and avoids internal jargon. |\\r\\n| **Questions and pauses** | Asks a genuine decision and gives an appropriate chance to answer. |\\r\\n| **Boundaries** | Shows what the information leaves open and why a tempting move fails. |\\r\\n| **Progression** | Each operation has a prerequisite, a reason to appear, and adequate practice. |\\r\\n| **Transfer** | Fresh questions require the taught skill, with reasoned feedback. |\\r\\n| **Tone and warmth** | Expects effort, supports the next action, and never mocks uncertainty. |\\r\\n| **Presentation** | Examples, comparisons, notation, and interactions clarify the reasoning. |\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not treat a high total as proof of an identical voice. Use the original source and Joshua\'s response to calibrate the subjective feel. His concrete corrections override a score.\\r\\n\\r\\n## A reusable writing brief\\r\\n\\r\\nUse this when giving another writer or agent the task. Supply the actual source, lesson scope, prerequisite knowledge, and approved method along with it.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nWrite this LSAT material in Joshua\'s selected teaching voice.\\r\\nRead wiki/teaching-voice.md, references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md,\\r\\nand wiki/COPY-CORRECTIONS.md before drafting.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep the reader beside the teacher. Start with the ordinary meaning of\\r\\nthe idea, then make it concrete with an original, intuitive example.\\r\\nShow each small inference in natural language. Ask the question a learner\\r\\nwould actually need to answer here. When the question is practice, leave\\r\\nroom for an attempt before revealing the reasoning.\\r\\n\\r\\nVary sentence length by purpose. Let explanations breathe and use short\\r\\nsentences to settle a consequence or a limit. Use contractions naturally.\\r\\nTeach the technical term when there is a clear idea to attach it to.\\r\\nRepeat an anchor only when the repetition changes the learner\'s view.\\r\\nShow a tempting mistake and how to detect it when that distinction matters.\\r\\n\\r\\nPreserve Joshua\'s method, the exact logical strength, complete conditions,\\r\\nand the selected topic scope. Give fresh practice with explained answers.\\r\\nDo not copy the reference\'s examples, jokes, personal claims, or procedural\\r\\ncounts. No em dashes, hype, invented evidence, internal stage language,\\r\\nor decorative catchphrases. Light humor is optional and must help the lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\nRead the result aloud, check every inference, and review the student-facing\\r\\nprompt and answer states. If the reader cannot hear why the next thought\\r\\nfollows, revise the explanation before polishing the surface.\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## Keep this reference current\\r\\n\\r\\nThis file is the detailed method reference, not a second canonical brand voice. [Teaching voice](../wiki/teaching-voice.md) remains the router. [COPY-CORRECTIONS](../wiki/COPY-CORRECTIONS.md) remains the record of demonstrated wording failures. Add Joshua\'s later calibration to the relevant section here rather than creating competing LSAT voice documents.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe project-owned `lsat-u-voice` skill reads this standard. Recap and bootcamp workflows also read it explicitly. An older vendor voice skill describes a different writer blend; it must not override this Joshua-selected standard in this project. Managed plugin caches are preserved rather than silently rewritten.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source archive is immutable. Future evidence or revised attachments should be recorded as a separate generation with provenance, not written over the original.\\r\\n# Copy corrections\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery student-facing wording fix, with the reason it was wrong. Read this before\\r\\nwriting or editing copy for LSAT U so the same mistake is not made twice.\\r\\n\\r\\nCompanion to [[teaching-voice]], which says how the writing should sound. This\\r\\nsays what has actually gone wrong and why.\\r\\n\\r\\nStarted 2026-09-07 from a Read, Recall, Colour pass. Add to it every time a\\r\\ncorrection is made.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The rules these corrections came from\\r\\n\\r\\nThree rules already existed and all three leaked anyway, because each was\\r\\nenforced on the components that happened to exist when it was written. A surface\\r\\nadded later starts uncovered.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** [[teaching-voice]], Core voice.\\r\\n- **No internal vocabulary in student copy.** `projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/CONTEXT.md`\\r\\n  carries the glossary and marks what to avoid.\\r\\n- **Every CSS token a stylesheet uses must be defined in it.** `projects/lsatu/CLAUDE.md`.\\r\\n\\r\\nGuards now live with the content rather than with each component:\\r\\n`content/instructions-voice.test.ts` checks the authored instructions, so every\\r\\nsurface that renders them is covered, including surfaces not written yet.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Corrections\\r\\n\\r\\n### Conditional opening: define the words before using them (2026-10-03)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua\'s marked browser paragraphs used “direction” and “guarantee” before making their meaning clear. The purpose paragraph also described an argument accepting more than its information supports without showing what that meant. Teach what a rule lets you conclude in plain language, then attach the vocabulary to a concrete relationship. Explain sufficient as enough and necessary as required before relying on those roles. Show what the must-arrow records and why English clause order does not determine the two sides.\\r\\n\\r\\n2026-10-03 clarification: explicitly distinguish the indicator from the complete condition it refers to. Sufficient goes left; necessary goes right. The indicator itself is not a condition in the diagram. Show the same relationship with if at the beginning and in the middle, and show necessary targets both before and after requirement language. Neither sentence position nor the words immediately following the indicator determine placement. Preserve if versus only if as different complete expressions.\\r\\n\\r\\nA rule describes what would follow **if** a condition were true; it does not say that condition happened. Bold that “if” and use meaningful in-view motion to expose the connection, with a static reduced-motion equivalent. Replace compressed ready-order wording with a natural full sentence. Give each paragraph and interaction a specific teaching job. These corrections supplement the canonical voice standard rather than adding a new writing register.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Generic reasoning prompts → concrete numbered demonstrations (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua marked four parts of the V6 opening: \\"Read each whole idea,\\" \\"Find what the statements guarantee,\\" the abstract first sentence about information, and the paragraph combining application and linking. They named goals without showing a useful action or explanation. Replace them with numbered, separate scenarios. Show the fact and rule that prove a conclusion about one case; separately show two matching rules and their new conditional conclusion. Labels should identify actual inputs or outputs. Review the whole note for repeated umbrella instructions and make task instructions executable. This follows the teaching voice: specific, concrete, short sentences, with air between distinct ideas.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Fact and rule definitions must explain the inference (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua rejected definitions that remained abstract and an explanation that did not clearly distinguish applying a rule from linking rules. Define the inputs with examples, then show the matching step and exact output. A case fact plus a rule proves something about that case. Two connecting rules produce another conditional rule without establishing a case exists. Adding a fact to the chain is a separate step. Explain all four fact situations and a hidden chain revealed by contraposition rather than leaving them implicit in an interactive model. Rules include general logical relationships, not only policies or obligations.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Boxed `L -> R` → bold teaching notation **L → R** (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua rejected the recap\'s small monospace arrow inside a pale code box. It looked like implementation text and weakened the explanation. Use a real, clearly weighted arrow in ordinary teaching typography. Explain its complete conditions before shortening them. The Some, Most, and All reference also governs the progression: introduce the whole idea, develop the individual components, then compare and combine them. A visual refresh must review that sequence, not only colors and boxes.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Concept lesson\\" → the actual reasoning title (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe recap preview exposed an internal label above the student lesson. Joshua explicitly rejected it. Use a title such as \\"Facts, Rules, and What Follows\\" and headings that teach the reasoning. Keep production labels, version metadata, and design commentary in private records. Check the rendered HTML, since its shell can introduce wording absent from the Markdown source.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Recall Rephrase Colour\\" → \\"Read, Recall, Colour\\"\\r\\nThe door\'s heading was hardcoded to a name the product does not have, one line\\r\\nunder a chip reading \\"Read, Recall, Colour\\". \\"Rephrase\\" belongs to a different\\r\\nActivity, Conditional Rephrase. A test asserted the wrong name, which is why\\r\\n2,600 passing tests never caught it.\\r\\n**Lesson:** when a test pins a string, check the string is right, not just that\\r\\nit matches.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Intake only. Nothing comes back out yet…\\" → plain instruction\\r\\nClinical and abstract, and the sentence then told her to read \\"with full\\r\\nintonation\\" while step one is silent reading. The clause that made intonation\\r\\ninternal, \\"hear it naturally in your head\\", had been dropped in an earlier edit.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a word like \\"intake\\" reads as jargon. And when copy is trimmed,\\r\\ncheck what the trimmed clause was load-bearing for.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Three beats through the stimulus\\" → \\"Three steps\\"\\r\\n\\"Beat\\" is the internal code name for one of the four method steps. The glossary\\r\\nsays students see **step**. The interface ten pixels below labelled the same four\\r\\nthings Step 1 to Step 4, so the page used two names for one thing.\\r\\n**Lesson:** never let an implementation name reach the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"22 pieces to read\\" → line removed\\r\\nA **piece** is one chunk, roughly a sentence, and the instructions on that same\\r\\npage use the word that way. The count was of stimuli, so \\"22 pieces\\" read as 22\\r\\nsentences.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a unit word must mean one thing per surface. Check what a word\\r\\nalready means on the page before reusing it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"say it back\\" → \\"tell it back\\", \\"The Read\\" → \\"The Recall\\"\\r\\nThe library door still carried both retired names. \\"The Read\\" was step four\'s\\r\\nformer name and collided with step one, which is why it was renamed.\\r\\n**Lesson:** a rename is not finished until every row carries it.
