text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp/src/bootcamps/conditionals/components/CounterexampleLab.tsx\n@@\n import { useId, useState } from 'react';\n+\n+const comparisons = [\n+  { sentence: 'Only stamped envelopes go into the dispatch tray.', same: true, reason: 'Only makes a stamp necessary for an envelope in the tray. An envelope in the tray must be stamped. A stamped envelope can still be elsewhere.' },\n+  { sentence: 'An envelope goes into the dispatch tray if it is stamped.', same: false, reason: 'If now makes the stamp sufficient for going into the tray. This sends every stamped envelope there. The original rule allowed stamped envelopes elsewhere.' },\n+  { sentence: 'The only envelopes in the dispatch tray are stamped envelopes.', same: true, reason: 'The only refers to envelopes in the tray. Being in the tray is enough to establish a stamp, just as in the original rule.' },\n+  { sentence: 'An envelope goes into the dispatch tray only if it is stamped.', same: true, reason: 'Only if makes being stamped a requirement for going into the tray. It does not promise a place in the tray to every stamped envelope.' },\n+];\n+\n+export function RuleComparisonLab() {\n+  const [index, setIndex] = useState(0);\n+  const [answers, setAnswers] = useState<Record<number, boolean>>({});\n+  const [explain, setExplain] = useState(false);\n+  const question = useId();\n+  const item = comparisons[index];\n+  const answer = answers[index];\n+  return <div className=\"co-comparison-lab\">\n+    <p>You now know both groups. Set the group names aside and read what each sentence promises.</p>\n+    <p className=\"co-kicker\">Keep this original rule</p><blockquote>Every envelope in the dispatch tray is stamped.</blockquote>\n+    <p>An envelope in the tray has to be stamped. A stamped envelope could still be elsewhere. Use that possible case to check each new version.</p>\n+    <div className=\"co-word-tabs\" role=\"group\" aria-label=\"Wording variations\">{comparisons.map((_, i) => <button type=\"button\" key={i} aria-pressed={index === i} onClick={() => { setIndex(i); setExplain(false); }}>Version {i + 1}</button>)}</div>\n+    <blockquote>{item.sentence}</blockquote><h3 id={question}>Does this preserve the original rule, or reverse it?</h3>\n+    <div className=\"co-choices\" role=\"group\" aria-labelledby={question}><button type=\"button\" aria-pressed={answer === true} onClick={() => setAnswers({ ...answers, [index]: true })}>Same rule</button><button type=\"button\" aria-pressed={answer === false} onClick={() => setAnswers({ ...answers, [index]: false })}>Reversed rule</button></div>\n+    <div role=\"status\">{answer !== undefined && <div className=\"co-feedback\"><strong>{answer === item.same ? 'The meaning matches your choice.' : 'Read the starting condition again.'}</strong><p>{item.reason}</p></div>}</div>\n+    {Object.keys(answers).length === comparisons.length && <div className=\"co-case-takeaway\"><h3>One word can change what follows</h3><p>Compare versions 2 and 4. Before opening the explanation, say what adding only did to the role of the stamp.</p><button type=\"button\" aria-expanded={explain} onClick={() => setExplain(!explain)}>Compare if with only if</button>{explain && <p>If makes the stamp enough for going into the tray. Only if makes it required for going into the tray. The stamp moved from the sufficient role to the necessary role. That's why reading the complete expression matters.</p>}</div>}\n+  </div>;\n+}\n*** End Patch"));

No workshop.' },\n+  { film: false, workshop: false, label: 'No film. No workshop.' },\n+  { film: true, workshop: true, label: 'Film showing. Workshop underway.' },\n+];\n+\n+export function NegativeCaseLab() {\n+  const [selected, setSelected] = useState<number[]>([]);\n+  const [checked, setChecked] = useState(false);\n+  const [workshopAnswer, setWorkshopAnswer] = useState<boolean | null>(null);\n+  const id = useId();\n+  const correct = selected.length === 2 && selected.includes(0) && selected.includes(1);\n+  return <div className=\"co-negative-lab\">\n+    <p>Let's take the same reasoning into a sentence whose required condition contains a negative. Accept this rule for the exercise:</p>\n+    <blockquote>If a room is showing a film, it is not hosting a workshop.</blockquote>\n+    <p>Use <strong>F</strong> for showing a film and <strong>W</strong> for hosting a workshop. Our rule is <strong>F → ~W</strong>. A film requires the absence of a workshop. We haven't said a film is the only reason a room might have no workshop.</p>\n+    <div className=\"co-given-fact\"><span className=\"co-kicker\">Given fact</span><strong>This room is not hosting a workshop: ~W.</strong></div>\n+    <h3 id={id}>Which possible rooms fit both the rule and that fact? Select every one that fits.</h3>\n+    <div className=\"co-room-options\" role=\"group\" aria-labelledby={id}>{rooms.map((room, index) => <button type=\"button\" key={room.label} aria-pressed={selected.includes(index)} onClick={() => { setSelected(items => items.includes(index) ? items.filter(i => i !== index) : [...items, index]); setChecked(false); }}><span className=\"co-room-drawing\" aria-hidden=\"true\"><i data-lit={room.film}/><b data-active={room.workshop}>W</b></span><span>{room.label}</span></button>)}</div>\n+    <button type=\"button\" className=\"co-primary\" disabled={selected.length === 0} onClick={() => setChecked(true)}>Check these possibilities</button>\n+    <div role=\"status\">{checked && <div className=\"co-feedback\"><strong>{correct ? 'Both film possibilities remain open.' : selected.includes(2) ? 'A workshop conflicts with the given fact.' : 'There is another case that fits.'}</strong><p>{selected.includes(2) ? \"The fact says no workshop. A film and a workshop would also break the original rule. Remove that room, then check the others.\" : \"A film with no workshop fits. No film with no workshop fits too. Both keep the rule true and satisfy the given fact, so ~W establishes neither F nor ~F. We know there is no workshop; we don't know whether there is a film.\"}</p></div>}</div>\n+    {checked && correct && <div className=\"co-case-takeaway\"><h3>Change the fact: now a workshop is underway.</h3><p>The rule stays F → ~W. Could this room also be showing a film?</p><div className=\"co-choices\"><button type=\"button\" aria-pressed={workshopAnswer === true} onClick={() => setWorkshopAnswer(true)}>Yes, it could.</button><button type=\"button\" aria-pressed={workshopAnswer === false} onClick={() => setWorkshopAnswer(false)}>No, it could not.</button></div><div role=\"status\">{workshopAnswer !== null && <p>{workshopAnswer ? \"A film would require no workshop. That conflicts with our new fact that a workshop is underway, so a film is ruled out.\" : \"A film would require no workshop, but a workshop is underway. That rules out a film. In symbols, W → ~F. Negating ~W gives W, which is why this is the contrapositive.\"}</p>}</div></div>}\n+  </div>;\n+}\n*** End Patch"));

An order has been packed. A guest has a ticket. We can ask whether either condition holds in a particular case.</p>\\r\\n      <p>A <strong>conditional statement</strong> tells us that if one condition is true, another has to be true too. It gives us a rule we can use, even before we know whether either condition is true in a particular case.</p>\\r\\n      <p className=\\"co-if-inline\\">We aren\'t saying the first condition happened. We\'re asking what would follow <strong>if</strong> it did.</p>\\r\\n      <HypotheticalFigure/>\\r\\n      <h3>Why learn this?</h3><p>On the LSAT, you need to distinguish what the information proves from what it leaves open. A conditional rule can help you prove a conclusion. An argument can also misuse the rule and reach a conclusion it hasn\'t proved. We\'ll practice telling those apart.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Let\'s read one rule.</p><blockquote>{orderRule}</blockquote>\\r\\n      <p>For this rule, the ready label makes packing certain. A ready order that hasn\'t been packed would break the stated relationship. That\'s what we mean by a <strong>guarantee</strong> here.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Compare that with “Ready orders are usually packed.” Usually allows an exception. Our if/then rule doesn\'t. We are working with the rule as given; we aren\'t claiming that every shop in real life follows it.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Does the rule itself tell us that an actual order is marked ready?\\" options={[\'Yes, at least one order is marked ready.\', \'No, it tells us what would follow if an order were marked ready.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'You added a case fact. The rule connects the conditions but has not reported an order with that label.\', \'The imagined ready order lets us understand the rule. We need a separate fact to establish that an actual order has the label.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>Now let\'s take the two conditions one at a time.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={2} label=\\"Sufficient means enough\\" title=\\"One condition gives you enough\\">\\r\\n      <blockquote>{orderRule}</blockquote><p>The <strong>if-part</strong> is the <strong>sufficient condition</strong>. Sufficient means enough. Knowing an order is marked ready is enough, under this rule, to know it has been packed.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-role-exhibit\\"><span>Sufficient</span><strong>Marked ready for pickup</strong><p>Enough to establish packing</p></div>\\r\\n      <p>The ready label might be present. That is when we can <strong>use</strong>, or activate, the rule in its stated direction.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Order E is marked ready. With the rule, that is enough to establish that E has been packed.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>We\'ll now keep this job in mind while changing the wording.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={3} label=\\"The sufficient family\\" title=\\"Different words can preserve the same rule\\">\\r\\n      <p>An <strong>indicator</strong> is an expression that helps you recognize a conditional relationship. It has not said every voucher recipient wears a blue badge.\']}/>\\r\\n      <details className=\\"cr-extension\\"><summary>Two more Group 1 expressions</summary><p><strong>Where</strong> can state a relationship across locations: “Where a collection point operates, parcels can be returned.” An operating collection point establishes the availability of returns there. The pump being on does not establish that the fountain runs.</p><p><strong>Requires</strong> directly names a requirement: “Entry requires a current pass.” Preserve current. <strong>Always</strong> needs the sentence\'s subject and scope: “The upstairs room is always quiet when the door is shut.” Here a shut door establishes quiet, not the other way around.</p><p><strong>Only</strong> and <strong>the only</strong> are different complete expressions. “Only packed orders are marked ready” and “The only orders marked ready are packed” both tell us that a ready order is packed.</p></details>\\r\\n      <p>We can now recognize both roles before writing any symbols. Each can tell us that if one condition holds, another must hold. A sentence about what usually happens leaves room for exceptions; a conditional rule makes its consequence certain whenever its sufficient condition holds.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Read the arrow as <strong>must</strong>. The sufficient condition goes on the left. The necessary condition goes on the right. If the left condition is true, the right condition must be true too. The arrow doesn\'t say which event happened first, and it doesn\'t establish that one event caused the other.</p>\\r\\n    </Section>\\r\\n    <Section title={first ? \'Different wording can make the same rule\' : \'Read it as a requirement\'}>\\r\\n      {first ? <>\\r\\n        <p>Suppose a studio has this rule: every painting with a silver seal has been inspected. Having the seal is enough to establish inspection. Let\'s keep that meaning and change the wording.</p>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"co-word-comparison\\"><div><blockquote>If a painting has a silver seal, it has been inspected.</blockquote><p>If what? It has a silver seal. That complete idea goes on the left.</p></div><div><blockquote>A painting has been inspected whenever it has a silver seal.</blockquote><p>Whenever what? It has a silver seal. The sufficient condition comes later in this sentence, but it still goes on the left.</p></div></div>\\r\\n        <Arrow left=\\"Has silver seal\\" right=\\"Has been inspected\\"/>\\r\\n        <p>The indicator can appear at the beginning or in the middle. Sentence position doesn\'t choose the side of the arrow. Find the idea the expression refers to, then ask what the sentence tells you if that idea is true.</p>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Each painting with a silver seal has been inspected. Did changing every to each change the rule?\\">\\r\\n          <p>No. Each still covers every painting with that seal. A painting with the seal that hadn\'t been inspected would break either statement. Keep has silver seal on the left and has been inspected on the right.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n        <p>Some wording presents a rule: <strong>if, when, whenever</strong>. Some covers a whole group: <strong>all, each, any, every</strong>. Read each in its sentence. Any in “Do you have any paint?” asks a question; it doesn\'t give us a rule.</p>\\r\\n        <p>Other sentences promise an outcome: “A silver seal ensures the painting has been inspected” or “A silver seal implies the painting has been inspected.” Here, the promised outcome is inspection. Ensures and implies express the arrow between the two complete ideas. Leads to, will, and always can also express a definite result in a rule, but the word alone doesn\'t settle the meaning. “The studio will open tomorrow” gives us no sufficient condition to put on the left.</p>\\r\\n        <p>We\'ll now examine the Group 1 expressions individually. Keep asking what each sentence makes sufficient, rather than sorting words without their meaning.</p>\\r\\n      </> : <>\\r\\n        <p>A useful way to read the whole rule is: <strong>the left condition requires the right condition</strong>. Suppose borrowing a studio camera requires a current membership. What is required for borrowing? A current membership. That\'s the necessary condition.</p>\\r\\n        <div className=\\"co-word-comparison\\"><div><blockquote>Borrowing a studio camera requires a current membership.</blockquote><p>The required idea comes after requires. Find the whole idea: a current membership.</p></div><div><blockquote>A current membership is required to borrow a studio camera.</blockquote><p>The same required idea now comes first. Moving it in the sentence hasn\'t changed what borrowing requires.</p></div></div>\\r\\n        <Arrow left=\\"Borrows studio camera\\" right=\\"Has current membership\\"/>\\r\\n        <ThinkPause prompt=\\"Mina has a current membership. Does this rule tell us she borrowed a camera?\\">\\r\\n          <p>No. Membership is something borrowing requires. Mina could have the membership and never borrow a camera. The rule tells us what we need if she borrows; having what she needs doesn\'t tell us she did.</p>\\r\\n        </ThinkPause>\\r\\n        <p>Notice the meaning shared by <strong>requires, necessitates, depends on,</strong> and <strong>relies on</strong> when they express a strict requirement. Find what the sentence says is required <strong>for the other condition</strong>. Then check that your arrow keeps that requirement on the right.</p>\\r\\n      </>}\\r\\n    </Section>\\r\\n    {IndicatorSections({ id })}\\r\\n    <Section title={first ? \'Find the target, then place it\' : \'Find the requirement, then place it\'}>\\r\\n      <p>{first\\r\\n        ? \\"Add what to the indicator when that gives you a sensible question. The target can come before or after the expression, so check its meaning in the complete sentence.\\"}</p>\\r\\n      <p>This is the <strong>What Test</strong>. The question helps you find the indicator\'s complete target before choosing its side of the arrow. Keep any words that limit which people, objects, places, or occasions the sentence covers. The question finds the idea; the whole sentence tells you what that idea does.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Work through the expressions below. First choose the complete target. Identify both complete ideas, choose the sufficient one for the left, and check whether your diagram says what the sentence says.</p>\\r\\n      <p>If you know the meaning but hesitate over the arrow, imagine the left condition is true. '{"chunk_id":"8d8b06","wall_time_seconds":1.5113718,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":7016,"output":"    <ReferenceStep number={1} label=\\"Start with meaning\\" title=\\"What does a conditional tell you?\\">\\r\\n      <p>A <strong>condition</strong> is an idea that can be true or false. You win a raffle. You get a bicycle. We can ask whether either condition holds in a particular case.</p>\\r\\n      <p>A <strong>conditional statement</strong> tells us that if one condition is true, another has to be true too. It gives us a rule we can use, even before we know whether either condition is true in a particular case.</p>\\r\\n      <p className=\\"co-if-inline\\">We aren\'t saying the first condition happened. We\'re asking what would follow <strong>if</strong> it did.</p>\\r\\n      <HypotheticalFigure/>\\r\\n      <h3>Why learn this?</h3><p>On the LSAT, you need to distinguish what the information proves from what it leaves open. A conditional rule can help you prove a conclusion. An argument can also misuse the rule and reach a conclusion it hasn\'t proved. We\'ll practice telling those apart.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Let\'s read one rule.</p><blockquote>{raffleRule}</blockquote>\\r\\n      <p>Under this rule, winning the raffle makes getting a bicycle certain. Winning without getting one would break the stated relationship. That is what we mean by a <strong>guarantee</strong> here.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Compare that with “If you win the raffle, you usually get a bicycle.” Usually allows an exception. Our rule does not. Take the stated rule as given; we are asking what it tells us, not whether a real organizer keeps a promise.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Does the rule itself tell us that you actually win the raffle?\\" options={[\'Yes, it says I win.\', \'No, it tells me what follows if I win.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'You added a case fact. The rule has not reported a win; it tells you what getting one would establish.\', \'Imagining a win helps us understand the rule. We need a separate fact to establish that you actually win.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>Now let\'s take the two conditions one at a time.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={2} label=\\"Sufficient means enough\\" title=\\"One condition gives you enough\\">\\r\\n      <blockquote>{raffleRule}</blockquote><p>The <strong>if-part</strong> is the <strong>sufficient condition</strong>. Sufficient means enough. Knowing you win is enough, under this rule, to know you get a bicycle.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-role-exhibit\\"><span>Sufficient</span><strong>Win the raffle</strong><p>Enough to establish getting a bicycle</p></div>\\r\\n      <p>You might win. You might not. The rule has not settled that question.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"You don\'t win the raffle. Could you still get a bicycle?\\" options={[\'Yes. Getting a bicycle is still possible.\', \'No. Without winning, getting a bicycle is impossible.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'You could buy one or receive one as a gift. You could also not get one. Neither case creates a winner who fails to get a bicycle, so both fit the rule.\', \'You made winning the only way to get a bicycle. The sentence gives one sufficient condition; it has not excluded other ways.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>Now suppose a fact gives us the sufficient condition. That is when we can <strong>use</strong>, or activate, the rule in its stated direction.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"You win the raffle. Do we need another fact to establish that you get a bicycle?\\" options={[\'Yes, we need another fact about the bicycle.\', \'No, the rule and the win establish it.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'The rule already covers the case in which you win. That fact meets its sufficient condition.\', \'Winning meets the sufficient condition. With the rule, that is enough to establish that you get a bicycle.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>We\'ll now keep this job in mind while changing the wording.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={3} label=\\"The sufficient family\\" title=\\"Different words can preserve the same rule\\">\\r\\n      <p>An <strong>indicator</strong> is an expression that helps you recognize a conditional relationship. These expressions can introduce an idea that is enough to establish another.</p>\\r\\n      <p>For the next examples, use a different stated rule: anyone who borrows a locker has a key. We will express that same connection in several ways. We haven\'t said everyone with a key borrows a locker.</p>\\r\\n      <WordFamily entries={sufficientFamily} role=\\"sufficient\\"/>\\r\\n      <p>When/whenever and any/anytime group related forms together. An ending changes the kind of case being discussed, but these examples keep the same connection. Read the whole sentence. A familiar word is a clue, not a substitute for its meaning.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Every guest wearing a blue badge receives a lunch voucher. Which complete idea is enough?\\" options={[\'Guest\', \'Guest wearing a blue badge\', \'Receives a lunch voucher\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'Guest alone drops the badge restriction and would make a claim about unbadged guests.\', \'The rule gives a voucher to every guest wearing a blue badge. Keep that qualification with the person.\', \'The voucher is what the rule establishes. It has not said every voucher recipient wears a blue badge.\']}/>\\r\\n      <details className=\\"cr-extension\\"><summary>Two more Group 1 expressions</summary><p><strong>Where</strong> can state a relationship across locations: “Where a collection point operates, parcels can be returned.” An operating collection point establishes the availability of returns there. Availability is not proof that someone made a return.</p><p><strong>The only</strong> needs its complete phrase: “The only notebooks on this shelf are hardback.” A notebook on the shelf is hardback. The sentence does not put every hardback notebook there.</p><p>These are part of your Group 1 work. Understand what the full expression covers before using its group as a placement shortcut.</p></details>\\r\\n      <p>We have seen what can be enough. Now let\'s name what that condition requires.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={4} label=\\"Necessary means required\\" title=\\"The other condition has to be there\\">\\r\\n      <blockquote>{raffleRule}</blockquote><p>The <strong>then-part</strong> is the <strong>necessary condition</strong>. Necessary means required. Under this rule, if you win, getting a bicycle has to follow.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-role-exhibit cr-required\\"><span>Necessary</span><strong>Get a bicycle</strong><p>Required whenever you win the raffle</p></div>\\r\\n      <p>Ask “required for what?” Here, a required result of winning under this rule. It is not a requirement you must satisfy before entering. The word necessary describes the relationship, not when the events occur.</p>\\r\\n      <p>We\'re looking at the same rule from its other side. Winning is enough to establish getting a bicycle. Getting a bicycle is the result the rule requires whenever you win.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Under our rule, what has to follow if you win?\\" options={[\'You get a bicycle.\', \'You ride the bicycle home.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'Getting a bicycle is the stated result. Winning without getting one would violate the rule.\', \'Riding is not part of this rule. The sentence establishes that you get a bicycle, not what you do with it.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>Necessary does not mean “the next event.” It means required by this relationship. A conditional need not tell you which event caused another, or when either happened.</p>\\r\\n      <p>As with sufficient language, the wording can vary while the relationship stays the same.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={5} label=\\"The necessary family\\" title=\\"Listen for what the sentence needs\\">\\r\\n      <p>Return to our locker rule. Borrowing a locker requires a key. The next expressions all identify that requirement in their complete sentences.</p>\\r\\n      <WordFamily entries={necessaryFamily} role=\\"necessary\\"/>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-contrast\\"><div><h3>If</h3><p>“You borrow a locker <strong>if</strong> you have a key.”</p><p>Having a key is enough for borrowing under this sentence.</p></div><div><h3>Only if</h3><p>“You borrow a locker <strong>only if</strong> you have a key.”</p><p>Having a key is required. This sentence has not made it enough.</p></div></div>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"A guest enters the lounge only if the guest has a current pass. What does entering establish?\\" options={[\'The guest has a current pass.\', \'Every guest with a pass enters.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'Only if identifies the current pass as required for entry. An entering guest therefore meets that requirement.\', \'You made the requirement enough. A guest could have a current pass and remain outside without violating the sentence.\']}/>\\r\\n      <details className=\\"cr-extension\\"><summary>More Group 2 forms, with the sentence intact</summary><p><strong>Only when</strong> and <strong>only where</strong> can restrict the occasions or places of an outcome: “The fountain runs only when its pump is on.” A running fountain requires an operating pump. The pump being on does not establish that the fountain runs.</p><p><strong>Requires</strong> directly names a requirement: “Entry requires a current pass.” Preserve current. <strong>Always</strong> needs the sentence\'s subject and scope: “The upstairs room is always quiet when the door is shut.” Here a shut door establishes quiet, not the other way around.</p><p><strong>Only</strong> and <strong>the only</strong> are different complete expressions. “Only people who get a bicycle win this raffle” and “The only people who win this raffle are people who get a bicycle” both preserve the rule: winning establishes getting a bicycle.</p></details>\\r\\n      <p>We can now recognize both roles before writing any symbols. Next, let\'s see what happens when a requirement is missing.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={6} label=\\"A missing requirement\\" title=\\"What if the requirement is missing?\\" dark>\\r\\n      <ContrapositiveDiscovery/>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={7} label=\\"The four situations\\" title=\\"Keep what follows separate from what stays open\\">\\r\\n      <p>Change the fact about your outcome while keeping the rule. Treat each fact as settled, not as a report that you are still waiting. Decide what it establishes before comparing the explanation.</p>\\r\\n      <FourCaseExplorer/>\\r\\n      <p>Starting from getting a bicycle and concluding that you win is the tempting <strong>reverse</strong>. Starting from not winning and concluding that you do not get a bicycle is the tempting <strong>inverse</strong>. Neither follows from this rule alone.</p>\\r\\n      <p>The contrapositive starts from <strong>not getting a bicycle</strong> and establishes <strong>not winning the raffle</strong>. Its reasoning depends on the missing required result, not on reversing whichever words happen to appear.</p>\\r\\n      <p>We now understand the relationship in words. Symbols will let us record that understanding without carrying every word of the sentence.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={8} label=\\"Build the first diagram\\" title=\\"Give the relationship a shorter form\\">\\r\\n      <p>Put the sufficient condition on the <strong>left</strong>, the necessary condition on the <strong>right</strong>, and a <strong>must arrow</strong> between them.</p>\\r\\n      <RuleDiagram left=\\"Sufficient: enough\\" right=\\"Necessary: required\\"/>\\r\\n      <p>The arrow means the left condition requires the right. It does not mean the left caused the right, or that the right happens later.</p>\\r\\n      <h3>Which idea goes on which side?</h3>\\r\\n      <p>The indicator helps you find a condition\'s job. Once you\'ve found that job, place the <strong>complete condition</strong> on its side of the arrow. We don\'t put the word if or only if in the diagram.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-contrast\\"><div><h3>Left: sufficient</h3><p>This is the condition that\'s enough to establish the other one. Group 1 expressions such as <strong>if, when, all, every</strong> and <strong>any</strong> can identify this condition.</p><p>“All people who borrow a locker have a key.” All refers to <strong>people who borrow a locker</strong>. For someone in that group, having a key follows. Borrowing goes left.</p></div><div><h3>Right: necessary</h3><p>This is what the sufficient condition requires. Group 2 expressions such as <strong>only if, requires</strong> and <strong>must</strong> can identify the requirement.</p><p>“Borrowing a locker requires a key.” What is required? <strong>Having a key.</strong> That condition goes right.</p></div></div>\\r\\n      <RuleDiagram left=\\"Borrows a locker\\" right=\\"Has a key\\"/>\\r\\n      <p>Read it back: if someone borrows a locker, they have a key. The arrow records that connection. It hasn\'t told us that everyone with a key borrows a locker.</p>\\r\\n      <h3>The sentence can move. The roles stay the same.</h3>\\r\\n      <p>Compare these two versions of our raffle rule. The indicator is bold; the complete idea it refers to is in brackets.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-language-pair\\"><p><strong>If</strong> [you win the raffle], you get a bicycle.</p><p>You get a bicycle <strong>if</strong> [you win the raffle].</p><span>If identifies the sufficient condition in both sentences.</span></div>\\r\\n      <p>In the second sentence, if appears in the middle. Its condition comes last, but winning is still enough to establish getting a bicycle. That condition still goes left. Don\'t let the first phrase in English choose the first side of your diagram.</p>\\r\\n      <RuleDiagram left=\\"Win the raffle\\" right=\\"Get a bicycle\\"/>\\r\\n      <p>Now try the same move with a requirement.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-language-pair\\"><p><strong>Only</strong> [people with a key] borrow a locker.</p><p>A person borrows a locker <strong>only if</strong> [they have a key].</p><span>Only and only if identify the necessary condition here.</span></div>\\r\\n      <p>Both sentences say locker borrowers have a key. In the first, only is at the beginning. In the second, only if is in the middle. Having a key is required in both, so it goes right. <strong>If</strong> and <strong>only if</strong> have different jobs; read only if as the whole expression.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"A person borrows a locker only if they have a key. Which condition goes on the right?\\" options={[\'Borrows a locker\', \'Has a key\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'Borrowing is what has the requirement. Ask what a locker borrower must have: a key. Borrowing goes left; having a key goes right.\', \'Having a key is required for borrowing. Only if appears in the middle, but it still identifies the necessary condition.\']}/>\\r\\n      <h3>The indicator can also follow its target</h3>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-language-pair\\"><p>[Having a key] is <strong>required</strong> for borrowing a locker.</p><p>Borrowing a locker <strong>requires</strong> [having a key].</p><span>Having a key is the requirement in both sentences.</span></div>\\r\\n      <p>The target is the complete idea the indicator refers to. It comes before required in the first sentence and after requires in the second. Having a key still goes right. We find it by asking what is required, not by taking whichever words come next.</p>\\r\\n      <p>You\'ll work through the less familiar expressions in their Group 1 and Group 2 lessons. For each one, keep the whole sentence: what is enough, and what does it require?</p>\\r\\n      <p>Let\'s build an original diagram slowly. First find the indicator, then draw the arrow, place the complete idea it refers to, and fill the other side.</p>\\r\\n      <IncrementalWriter/>\\r\\n      <p>Now move the if-clause: “You get a bicycle if you win the raffle.” The winning condition comes last in English but still goes left in the diagram. Its job has not changed.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Which diagram preserves the moved if-clause?\\" options={[\'Get bicycle → Win\', \'Win → Get bicycle\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'You let sentence order choose the arrow. The if-clause still makes winning enough for getting a bicycle.\', \'The sufficient condition is still winning. Where it appears in the sentence does not change what it establishes.\']}/>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={9} label=\\"Write and read the contrapositive\\" title=\\"Write the meaning you already understand\\">\\r\\n      <p>Win means you win the raffle. Get bicycle means you get a bicycle. Our original is Win → Get bicycle.</p>\\r\\n      <p>We already know that not getting a bicycle rules out winning. Write that as <strong>~Get bicycle → ~Win</strong>. The <strong>~</strong> sign means <strong>not</strong>. Not getting the outcome is different from not having received it yet.</p>\\r\\n      <p>To write a contrapositive from a diagram, reverse the two sides and negate <strong>both complete conditions</strong>. A condition already containing not loses that not when we negate it. Let\'s try all four patterns.</p>\\r\\n      <SignPatterns/>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-method\\"><p className=\\"co-kicker\\">The complete five-step routine</p><ol><li><strong>Find the indicator.</strong> Read its job in the whole sentence.</li><li><strong>Identify both complete ideas.</strong> Keep restrictions such as current or submitted by Friday.</li><li><strong>Place the roles.</strong> Sufficient goes left; necessary goes right. Choose labels you can read back.</li><li><strong>Write the contrapositive.</strong> Reverse the sides and negate both complete conditions.</li><li><strong>Read both in English.</strong> Compare them with what the original sentence actually requires.</li></ol></div>\\r\\n      <p>The original and its contrapositive describe the same relationship. If writing both helps you see that relationship, write both. If you can read the contrapositive from the original when it is relevant, you needn\'t copy it merely to have a second line.</p>\\r\\n      <p>Read an arrow forward to use its stated direction. To read its contrapositive, start from the right condition\'s absence and work back to the left condition\'s absence. That is a different move from reading the arrow backward unchanged.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={10} label=\\"Practical diagramming questions\\" title=\\"Use writing to make your reasoning easier to check\\">\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-faq\\">\\r\\n        <details><summary>When should I diagram?</summary><p>While learning, write enough to make your choices visible. A difficult sentence, several rules or a connection you keep rereading can be a reason to put the relationship on paper. With practice, you may hold a simple rule mentally. Use the writing to help the reasoning.</p></details>\\r\\n        <details><summary>How do I check whether my diagram is right?</summary><p>Read it back and compare the whole meaning. Did you keep each restriction? Does your arrow promise something the original leaves open? When a diagram is wrong, record the exact phrase and the mistake it produced. That gives you something specific to practice. Familiarity alone is not proof of correctness.</p></details>\\r\\n        <details><summary>What if writing takes time?</summary><p>Start by producing a correct, readable diagram. Speed is a later practice goal. Writing can reduce rereading, but it does not save time in every case. Compare how it helps on the sentences you are actually working through. First make the relationship accurate. Work on speed once you can explain why the arrow follows. </p></details>\\r\\n        <details><summary>Should I always write the contrapositive?</summary><p>You need to understand it every time. Write it when it helps you use the missing requirement, inspect your translation or connect rules. Otherwise, you may read that direction from the original. Extra notation should have a job.</p></details>\\r\\n        <aside className=\\"cr-training-note\\"><h3>Why this practice asks for both</h3><p>In the integrated drill, write or choose the original and the contrapositive. We\'re checking that you can produce both. Once that skill is reliable, a performance task need not require both lines for every rule.</p></aside>\\r\\n        <details><summary>How should I abbreviate the conditions?</summary><p>Use short labels that bring back the complete idea. W might mean win this raffle. Current pass may be clearer than a single letter if you\'re tracking several kinds of pass. Shortening should save writing without losing meaning. There is no fixed letter limit.</p></details>\\r\\n      </div>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Only envelopes with a paid stamp go into this tray. Someone wrote Paid stamp → In tray. What needs repairing?\\" options={[\'The labels need to be longer.\', \'The arrow makes the requirement enough.\', \'Nothing; the first phrase always goes left.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'Longer labels would not repair the direction. The tray requires a paid stamp, but a stamped envelope can remain outside it.\', \'Only restricts tray envelopes to ones with paid stamps. In tray → Paid stamp preserves that requirement; the proposed reverse promises tray placement to every stamped envelope.\', \'Sentence order does not determine diagram order. Only identifies the paid stamp as required for tray placement.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>That error came from the language. Let\'s inspect precisely which idea an indicator refers to.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={11} label=\\"Find the target\\" title=\\"Read the whole idea the indicator refers to\\">\\r\\n      <p>An indicator\'s <strong>target</strong> is the complete word or phrase it refers to. In “All guests wearing blue badges receive vouchers,” all refers to guests wearing blue badges, not guests alone.</p>\\r\\n      <p>The target often comes after its indicator. But often isn\'t always. Try these sentences in order.</p>\\r\\n      {targetExamples.map(item => <TargetReader item={item} key={item.label}/>)}\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-language-pair\\"><p>“Editor approval is required for publication.”</p><p>“Publication requires editor approval.”</p><span>Same requirement, different placement</span></div>\\r\\n      <p>Neither the closest noun nor the next word is a reliable target rule. Read which complete idea the sentence calls required. Then give that idea its role in the diagram.</p>\\r\\n      <p>When the wording still feels uncertain, we can test a proposed translation against an imagined case.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={12} label=\\"Check an interpretation\\" title=\\"Try the sentence from the inside\\">\\r\\n      <p>A <strong>Personalized If/Then</strong> lets you test what a proposed sufficient condition would establish. First read the ordinary meaning. Propose the sufficient idea. Imagine a case meeting it. Ask what the sentence now requires.</p>\\r\\n      <blockquote>Only people wearing helmets ride the studio bikes.</blockquote><p>The sentence restricts riders to people wearing helmets. Keep that meaning while trying each proposed starting point.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-personalized\\"><div><p className=\\"co-kicker\\">First proposed starting point</p><ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"If I\'m riding a studio bike, what does this sentence tell me?\\" options={[\'I am wearing a helmet.\', \'The helmet question is open.\']} correct={0} feedback={[\'The sentence puts every rider in the helmet-wearing group. Riding → Wearing helmet preserves that meaning.\', \'Only restricts who rides. If you meet the riding condition, the sentence does settle helmet wearing.\']}/></div><div><p className=\\"co-kicker\\">Try the other starting point</p><ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"If I\'m wearing a helmet, must I be riding a studio bike?\\" options={[\'Yes, the helmet proves riding.\', \'No, I could wear one without riding.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'You gave every helmet wearer a ride. The sentence restricts riders; it does not make all helmet wearers riders.\', \'A helmet wearer waiting beside a bike fits the sentence. Wearing helmet → Riding would add a promise the original did not make.\']}/></div></div>\\r\\n      <p>The first reading matches the sentence. The second proposed arrow fails because it rules out a case the original permits. Use the imagined situation to inspect meaning, not to supply extra facts from what usually happens.</p>\\r\\n      <h3>Use the What Test beside it</h3><p>Ask a sensible question about the expression: only what? People wearing helmets. What is required? Wearing a helmet. What is enough? Riding a studio bike, under this rule, establishes that requirement.</p>\\r\\n      <p>The What Test finds the complete target. The Personalized If/Then checks what your proposed direction says about a case. Use them together when one part of the translation is unclear.</p>\\r\\n      <p>We\'ve now read the relationship, understood its limits, written both directions and checked the language. Put those pieces together with fresh sentences.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n\\r\\n    <ReferenceStep number={13} label=\\"Use the whole process\\" title=\\"Build an original and its contrapositive\\">\\r\\n      <p>For each sentence, identify the indicator and both complete conditions. Choose the original diagram, then its contrapositive. Read both back before checking.</p>\\r\\n      <p>You can look back. The job here is to produce and inspect the reasoning, not to prove you memorized every expression on the first reading. The labels below keep the complete ideas visible while you choose the directions.</p>\\r\\n      <div className=\\"cr-integrated-grid\\">{referencePracticeItems.map((item, index) => <IntegratedItem item={item} number={index + 1} key={item.sentence}/>)}</div>\\r\\n      <p>If an answer needs revision, name the exact issue: lost qualification, wrong role, reversed arrow or incomplete negation. Then retry that item. Your targeted Group 1 and Group 2 work gives you more practice with individual expressions; this set checks whether the steps hold together.</p>\\r\\n    </ReferenceStep>\\r\\n    <section id=\\"reference-boundary\\" className=\\"cr-boundary co-section\\" data-reference-boundary data-toc data-toc-title=\\"Permission and instructions\\">\\r\\n      <p className=\\"co-kicker\\">Before the attached practice</p><h2>Keep what the sentence actually gives you</h2>\\r\\n      <p>The core process is now in place. One more distinction matters for the practice: a conditional can give permission or an instruction. Preserve that strength instead of turning it into a report of what someone did.</p>\\r\\n      <blockquote>Every guest with a ticket may use the cloakroom.</blockquote><p>May use gives permission here. A ticketed guest is allowed to use the cloakroom. The guest could keep their coat on and never go inside.</p>\\r\\n      <ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"Lena is a guest with a ticket. Do we know that she used the cloakroom?\\" options={[\'Yes, the ticket establishes that she used it.\', \'No, we know she is allowed to use it.\']} correct={1} feedback={[\'You turned permission into a completed action. Lena meets the condition for permission, but we have no fact reporting her use of the cloakroom.\', \'The rule gives Lena permission because she is a guest with a ticket. Whether she used the cloakroom remains open.\']}/>\\r\\n      <p>Now compare an instruction. “If your coat is wet, hang it on the rack” tells you what to do with a wet coat. ## assistant

The 70 pages contain useful teaching, but the navigation treats explanations, examples, recalls and individual questions as equivalent “lessons.” The largest problem is repeated coverage: orientation teaches almost the entire opening before the next three units teach it again.

**Recommendation: 9 reading pages and 4 practice checkpoints.** Keep the expression inventories, meaningful examples and feedback inside those pages. Do not make every expression, reminder or exercise another navigation destination.

### What currently produces 70 pages

| Unit | Pages | Actual composition |
|---|---:|---|
| Orientation | 26 | Original 13 stages expanded to 20 pages: stage 8 becomes 3; stage 13 becomes 6 individual exercises. Plus foundation recall, negative-room lab, permission/instructions, media recap, counterexample lab and mistake recap. |
| Sufficient/necessary | 9 | Six explanations, foundation recall, media recap and mistake recap. Substantial overlap with orientation’s definitions, four cases, diagram roles and interpretation check. |
| Group 1 | 17 | Two introductions, seven expression pages, six method/practice pages, recall deck and mistake recap. |
| Group 2 | 18 | Same 17-page structure, plus mixed-wording lab. |
| **Total** | **70** | Page count substantially exceeds distinct concepts. |

The six Group 1/2 method/practice pages are: target identification, complete condition, only/the only, diagram builder, legacy recall cards and a final meaning check. They recur in both groups.

Not every repeated example is waste. The problem is that repetition repeatedly restarts the teaching instead of asking the learner to retrieve or apply what they learned.

### Proposed reading sequence

| Page | Keep and combine | Practice before moving on |
|---|---|---|
| **1. What conditionals are** | Condition versus conditional; exceptionless rule versus “usually”; rule versus case fact; LSAT purpose. Approved raffle example. Fold the final rule/fact repair into this explanation. | Decide whether the rule establishes a win; apply a separately supplied fact. |
| **2. The sufficient condition** | Enough to establish the other condition. Winning is sufficient for getting a bicycle. Combine “enough” with “not the only way”; explain purchase/gift possibilities immediately. | Fresh sufficient-condition identification and a no-win case. |
| **3. The necessary condition** | Required **for what**; getting a bicycle is required whenever someone wins. Not a prerequisite to entering, not automatically earlier, not sufficient by itself. Combine archive/pass contrast and relationship-role explanation. | Identify the required result; reject the reverse with a compatible case. |
| **4. Read the must arrow** | Sufficient left, necessary right. “The left requires the right.” Original diagram, meaningful labels, English readback. Compare the raffle sentence with its moved if-clause. Neither word order nor causation determines the arrow. | Construct one diagram and repair a reversed one. |
| **5. Words that identify the sufficient condition** | All seven core Group 1 expressions, grouped within one page: **if, when, where, all, the only, every, any**. Preserve supplementary forms and sentence-specific nuances in an in-page expression selector. One common introduction, not seven repeated introductions. | Target and diagram attempts within each expression; foundation recall before a new example. |
| **6. Words that identify the necessary condition** | All seven core Group 2 expressions: **only, only if, only when, only where, always, requires, must**. Include extended requirement language. Keep obligation/permission distinct from actual compliance here. | Target-before/after comparison; recording-booth reservation check; required action versus completed action. |
| **7. Keep the whole meaning when the wording changes** | Combine complete-condition qualification, only versus the only, What Test, Personalized If/Then and target position. This is application after both families, not another full definition of each method. | Mixed unfamiliar sentences, loss-of-qualification distractors and equivalent-wording lab. |
| **8. What a missing requirement tells you** | Conceptual contrapositive plus all four starting facts on one coherent page. Two facts establish something; two leave the other condition open. Retain settled bicycle outcome clarification. | Four-case explorer; construct a counterexample to the reverse. |
| **9. Write and read the contrapositive** | Reverse and negate both complete conditions; existing negatives; four sign patterns; full method. Embed practical diagramming FAQ as optional help beside the activity. | Negative-room lab, followed by full original/contrapositive practice. |

The expression selectors should expose every expression by name, with its explanation and attempt. This preserves depth without an enormous scroll or seven separate navigation destinations.

### Four checkpoints between lessons

1. **After page 3: Rule, fact, enough, required.** Fresh cases and a counterexample. Establish the meaning before introducing notation.
2. **After page 5: Translate a sufficient statement.** Identify the full target, build the diagram and explain its direction. Use the existing Group 1 builder and appropriate fresh items.
3. **After page 7: Mixed wording.** Mix Group 1/2 so the heading cannot supply the answer. Include only/the only, moved targets, qualifications and modality.
4. **After page 9: Put the process together.** Existing six original-plus-contrapositive exercise pairs become one item-by-item practice destination, retaining answers and feedback.

These are four distinct skill transitions, which is why four checkpoints are justified. They are not four arbitrary extra pages.

### Existing practice worth preserving

- **25 unique reviewed flip cards:** 4 foundation, 10 Group 1, 11 Group 2. The foundation deck currently appears twice, so there are **29 card placements**, not 29 unique cards.
- **14 legacy recall examples:** seven per indicator group, in addition to the reviewed decks. Consolidate their best distinct sentences into retrieval/practice rather than requiring a second separate recall page.
- **14 target-selection examples and 14 diagram-builder examples:** seven per group in each collection. Keep these available within the family pages/checkpoints.
- Orientation already contains the **four-case explorer, three target-position examples, four symbolic sign-pattern questions and six paired original/contrapositive exercises**.
- The three new applied labs have distinct purposes: **ticket counterexample**, **two possible negative rooms**, **equivalent wording**. Keep them at the relevant checkpoints.
- Four opening units have **4 guided questions and 62 recorded drill items**: orientation 9; sufficient/necessary 9; Group 1 23; Group 2 21. These are existing teacher-assigned banks, not 62 additional reading pages.

All thirteen original skeleton concepts survive this arrangement. Their old order does not need to survive: Joshua now explicitly wants both definitions established before the indicator families.

One implementation issue must be handled deliberately: the current content belongs to four separate unit/progress contracts. A more coherent reading path must not silently reinterpret recorded completion, assignments or bank difficulty. The compression above is a curriculum recommendation, not authorization to migrate those records.

No app files or source notes changed during this audit.

requirement into a guarantee.', unitId: 'sufficient-necessary' },\n  { id: 'foundation-practice', type: 'drill', title: 'Enough, required, or still open?', description: 'Use fresh facts and build a original diagram and its contrapositive for six fresh sentences.', unitId: 'sufficient-necessary' },\n];\n\nexport function openingCourseStep(id?: string) {\n  return OPENING_COURSE_PATH.find(step => 'page' : undefined} to={url('lessons')} onClick={() => setOpen(false)}><BookOpen size={18}/>Lessons</Link>\n    <p>Practice</p><Link aria-current={view === 'practice' ? 'page' : undefined} to={url('practice')} onClick={() => setOpen(false)}><Sparkles size={18}/>Practice Drills</Link>\n    <Link aria-current={view === 'labs' ? 'page' : undefined} to={url('labs')} onClick={() => setOpen(false)}><Dumbbell size={18}/>Drill Lab</Link>\n    <p>Tools</p><Link aria-current={view === 'tools' ? 'page' : undefined} to={url('tools')} onClick={() => setOpen(false)}><Bookmark size={18}/>Flashcards</Link>\n  </nav>;\n  return <>\n    <aside className=\"oc-course-rail\"><Link className=\"oc-back\" to=\"/classroom\"><ArrowLeft size={15}/>Classroom</Link><div className=\"oc-brand\">Conditional logic</div>{navigation}</aside>\n    <div className=\"oc-mobile-nav\"><Link to={url('lessons')}>Conditional logic</Link><Sheet open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen}><SheetTrigger asChild><button type=\"button\"><Menu size={18}/>Course menu</button></SheetTrigger><SheetContent side=\"left\" className=\"oc-course-drawer\" aria-describedby={undefined}><SheetTitle>Conditional logic</SheetTitle>{navigation}</SheetContent></Sheet></div>\n  </>;\n}\n\nfunction CourseCard({ step, url }: { step: OpeningCourseStep; url: OpeningCourseUrl }) {\n  return <li className=\"oc-path-card\"><span className=\"oc-label\">{step.type}</span><h2>{step.title}</h2><p>{step.description}</p><Link className=\"oc-action\" to={url(step.id)}>{step.type === 'note' ? <BookOpen size={16}/> : <Dumbbell size={16}/>} {step.type === 'note' ? 'Read lesson' : 'View drill'}<ArrowRight size={16}/></Link></li>;\n}\n\nexport function OpeningCourseScreen({ view = 'lessons', run = false, url, steps = OPENING_COURSE_PATH, recordedPractice }: {\n  view?: string; run?: boolean; url: OpeningCourseUrl; steps?: OpeningCourseStep[]; recordedPractice?: ReactNode;\n}) {\n  const current = steps.find(step => step.id === view);\n  const [visited, setVisited] = useState<string[]>([]);\n  const root = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);\n  useEffect(() => {\n    if (current && (current.type === 'note' || run)) setVisited(prior => prior.includes(view) ? prior : [...prior, view]);\n    requestAnimationFrame(() => {\n      const heading = root.current?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[data-course-heading] h1');\n      heading?.focus({ preventScroll: true });\n      heading?.scrollIntoView?.({ block: 'start', behavior: 'instant' });\n    });\n  }, [view, run, current]);\n  const index = steps.findIndex(step => step.id === view);\n  const prior = steps[index - 1];\n  const next = steps[index + 1];\n  const list = view === 'labs' || view === 'practice' ? steps.filter(step => step.type === 'drill') : steps;\n  const isIndex = ['lessons', 'labs', 'practice'].includes(view);\n  return <div ref={root} className=\"oc-course-screen\">\n    {isIndex && <div className=\"oc-course-index\">\n      <div data-course-heading><PageHeader noBloom eyebrow={view === 'lessons' ? 'Introduction' : 'Practice'} title={view === 'lessons' ? 'Conditional reasoning.' : view === 'labs' ? 'Make the move yourself.' : 'Practice the reasoning.'} description={view === 'lessons' ? 'Learn one idea, use it, then build on it. The drills between lessons give you a chance to test the meaning before moving on.' : 'Make an attempt before reading the explanation. Name the mistake, repair it and try again.'}/></div>\n      {view === 'practice' && recordedPractice}\n      <ol className=\"oc-course-path\">{list.map(step => <CourseCard key={step.id} step={step} url={url}/>)}</ol>\n      {!list.length && <p>No opening lessons are available in this work.</p>}\n    </div>}\n    {view === 'tools' && <div className=\"oc-course-note\">\n      <div data-course-heading><PageHeader noBloom eyebrow=\"Tools\" title=\"Recall before you turn.\" description=\"Say the relationship in your own words. Turn the card to compare your reasoning.\"/></div>\n      <div className=\"co-opening\"><h2>Enough and required</h2><StudyDeck group=\"foundation\"/><h2>Sufficient-condition words</h2><StudyDeck group=\"group-1\"/><h2>Necessary-condition words</h2><StudyDeck group=\"group-2\"/></div>\n    </div>}\n    {current && <div className=\"oc-course-note\">\n      <Link className=\"oc-back\" to={url('lessons')}><ArrowLeft size={15}/>All lessons</Link>\n      <div data-course-heading><PageHeader noBloom eyebrow={current.type === 'note' ? 'Lesson' : run ? 'Drill' : 'Practice checkpoint'} title={current.title} description={current.description}/></div>\n      {current.type === 'drill' && !run && <section className=\"oc-drill-entry\"><h2>Make an attempt. Check the reasoning.</h2><ol><li>Read the rule and the exact question.</li><li>Choose or build your answer before checking.</li><li>Use the feedback to identify what you kept or changed.</li><li>Retry the case and explain your correction.</li></ol><p>These exercises are for practice. Opening a drill or revealing an explanation does not establish mastery.</p><Link className=\"oc-action\" to={url(view, true)}>Start drill<ArrowRight size={16}/></Link></section>}\n    </div>}\n    <div className=\"oc-course-bodies\">{steps.filter(step => visited.includes(step.id)).map(step => <div key={step.id} hidden={step.id !== view || (step.type === 'drill' && !run)} className=\"oc-course-body co-opening cr-sequence\"><OpeningCourseContent id={step.id}/></div>)}</div>\n    {current && (current.type === 'note' || run) && <nav className=\"oc-course-turn\" aria-label=\"Course navigation\">{prior ? <Link to={url(prior.id)}><span>Previous {prior.type === 'note' ? 'lesson' : 'drill'}</span><strong>{prior.title}</strong></Link> : <Link to={url('lessons')}>All lessons</Link>}{next ? <Link to={url(next.id)}><span>Next {next.type === 'note' ? 'lesson' : 'drill'}</span><strong>{next.title}<ArrowRight size={18}/></strong></Link> : <Link to={url('lessons')}>Return to lessons<ArrowRight size={18}/></Link>}</nav>}\n    {!isIndex && view !== 'tools' && !current && <div className=\"oc-course-note\"><h1>This lesson is not available here.</h1><Link to={url('lessons')}>Return to lessons</Link></div>}\n  </div>;\n}\n''',encoding='utf-8')\n'@ | python -","workdir":"C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os-projects/lsatu-conditional-bootcamp","max_output_tokens":1000}));

3 : 5);\\r\\n  const family = sections(source.props.children).find(child => child.type === WordFamily);\\r\\n  if (!family) throw new Error(`Missing approved ${group} supplementary family`);\\r\\n  return <details className=\\"co-practical-note\\"><summary>More expressions for the same relationship</summary>\\r\\n    <p>Use the stated rule: anyone who borrows a locker has a key. It does not record a scored attempt or establish mastery.</p>\\r\\n  </NoteSection>;\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\r\\nfunction Content({ id }: { id: string }) {\\r\\n  switch (id) {\\r\\n    case \'meaning\': return <ReferenceBody number={1} omitTransition/>;\\r\\n    case \'sufficient\': return <ReferenceBody number={2} omitTransition/>;\\r\\n    case \'necessary\': return <><ReferenceBody number={4} omitTransition/><ReferenceQuestion prompt=\\"You get a bicycle.
